questions.intro: Checking is for money you will spend soon: bills and everyday purchases. Savings is for money you are setting aside for later: goals and emergencies.
questions.question: Which money belongs in savings rather than checking?

choices.text: Money set aside for a laptop you plan to buy next spring
Money for this week's groceries
Money to pay this month's phone bill when it arrives next week
Cash for lunch tomorrow

questions.correct_answer: Money set aside for a laptop you plan to buy next spring
questions.feedback: Money for a later goal belongs in savings.

questions.intro: Interest on savings is money the bank pays you for keeping your money there. It is added to your balance.
questions.question: Leila earns 2% interest on her $500 savings for a year. What does "earning interest" mean here?

choices.text: The bank adds money to her account
The bank charges her 2% to hold her money
She owes the bank $10
Her $500 is locked until she turns 18

questions.correct_answer: The bank adds money to her account

misconceptions.B: Confuses interest earned with a fee

questions.feedback: 2% of $500 is $10, which the bank adds to her account.

questions.intro: Percent means "per hundred." To write a percent as a decimal, divide by 100 (move the decimal point two places left).
questions.question: What is 2% written as a decimal?
Using 0.02 for 2%, how much interest does $500 earn in one year?
Which statement is TRUE about money in an insured savings account?

choices.text: It always grows faster than prices rise
It can be withdrawn with no limits of any kind at every bank in the country
It earns the same interest at every bank
Its value in dollars does not go down because of market changes

questions.correct_answer: Its value in dollars does not go down because of market changes
questions.feedback: Insured deposits do not lose dollars to market swings, though inflation can still reduce what the money buys.

questions.intro: The interest rate is the yearly rate before compounding. APY (annual percentage yield) shows what you actually earn in a year once interest is added to your balance and itself earns interest (compounding). Banks must show APY for savings, so use APY to compare accounts.
questions.question:
Two savings accounts show:
Bank A: interest rate 4.00%, compounded monthly; APY 4.07%
Bank B: APY 4.05%
Which number should Mo use to compare them fairly?

choices.text: The APY of each account
The interest rate of Bank A and the APY of Bank B
The interest rate of each, ignoring APY
Whichever number is printed larger in the ad

questions.correct_answer: The APY of each account
questions.feedback: APY includes compounding, so comparing APY to APY is fair. Bank A (4.07%) earns slightly more than Bank B (4.05%).

questions.intro: APY is the actual percent your money grows in one year, so one year of earnings ≈ balance × APY.
questions.question: An account has an APY of 4.07%. About how much will $2,000 earn in one year if the rate stays the same and nothing is withdrawn?

misconceptions.D: Gives the balance, not the interest

questions.intro: APY (annual percentage yield) is the percent your money actually grows in one year. The stated interest rate is the yearly rate before compounding.
questions.question: Why is APY usually a little higher than the stated interest rate?

choices.text: Banks add a bonus to every account
APY includes extra deposits you plan to make later in the year
APY is the rate before taxes are added
Interest that is added during the year also earns interest

questions.correct_answer: Interest that is added during the year also earns interest
questions.feedback: With compounding, earlier interest earns interest too, so the yearly yield is above the stated rate.

questions.intro: Most savings accounts have variable rates: the bank can raise or lower them, often when market interest rates change. A certificate of deposit usually locks a rate for its term.
questions.question: A savings rate is "variable." What does that mean?

choices.text: The bank can change the rate over time
The rate is fixed until the account is closed
The rate depends on how many times you log in
The rate is negative in some months

questions.correct_answer: The bank can change the rate over time
questions.feedback: Variable means the bank may change it; past or advertised rates are not promises.

questions.question: An ad shows "5.00% APY*", and the fine print says "*on balances up to $1,000; 0.50% APY on the amount above $1,000." Sara deposits $5,000. About how much interest will she earn in one year?

questions.section_skill: Deposit insurance limits and ownership categories
questions.intro: The $250,000 limit applies per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. Money at two different banks is insured separately. (Two "brands" of the same bank are one bank for insurance purposes.)
questions.question: Marcus has $200,000 in an individual account at Bank A and $200,000 in an individual account at Bank B. Both banks are FDIC insured and separate. How much of his money is insured?

misconceptions.C: Applies one limit across different banks
misconceptions.A: Thinks large balances are never insured

questions.feedback: Each bank insures his $200,000 individually: $400,000 total.

questions.section_skill: Deposit insurance limits and ownership categories
questions.intro: Joint accounts are a separate ownership category from individual accounts. Each co-owner's share of joint accounts at one bank is insured up to $250,000.
questions.question: Sam and Pat own a joint account with $500,000 at one insured bank. Joint accounts are insured up to $250,000 per co-owner. How much is insured?

misconceptions.B: Applies one limit to the whole joint account

questions.feedback: Two co-owners × $250,000 = $500,000 of coverage, which covers the whole balance.

questions.section_skill: Deposit insurance limits and ownership categories
questions.question: Which product is covered by FDIC insurance when bought at an insured bank?

choices.text: Shares of an index fund
A cryptocurrency purchase
The contents of a safe deposit box
A 12-month certificate of deposit

questions.correct_answer: A 12-month certificate of deposit

misconceptions.A: Thinks funds sold at banks are insured
misconceptions.B: Thinks crypto at a bank is insured

questions.feedback: CDs are deposits. Investments, crypto assets, and safe deposit box contents are not insured deposits.

questions.section_skill: Deposit insurance limits and ownership categories
questions.intro: Only deposits at FDIC-insured banks (or NCUA-insured credit unions) are covered by deposit insurance. The FDIC warns consumers about companies that misrepresent their products as FDIC insured.
questions.question: A website for a company that sells crypto says, "Your funds are safe — like a bank." What should a careful saver conclude?

choices.text: The funds must be FDIC insured
The company is a federally chartered bank
The NCUA insures every crypto platform that operates in the United States
That claim does not mean the funds are FDIC insured

questions.correct_answer: That claim does not mean the funds are FDIC insured

misconceptions.A: Treats a comparison as a guarantee

questions.feedback: Comparisons to banks are not insurance. Check the FDIC's BankFind tool to see if an institution is an insured bank, and remember crypto assets are not deposits.

questions.section_skill: Deposit insurance limits and ownership categories
questions.question: Ella has $260,000 in one individual account at an insured bank and wants all of it insured. Which change would accomplish that most directly?

choices.text: Move $10,000 or more to an account at a different insured bank
Split it into two individual accounts at the same bank
Ask the bank to raise her personal limit
Withdraw the extra $10,000 and invest it in stocks for added safety

questions.correct_answer: Move $10,000 or more to an account at a different insured bank

misconceptions.B: Thinks multiple accounts in one category add coverage

questions.feedback: Coverage is per bank per category. Two individual accounts at the same bank share one $250,000 limit; a second bank adds coverage.

questions.section_skill: Choose and use payment methods safely: checks, electronic transfers, and payment apps
questions.intro: A check is a written order telling your bank to pay someone from your account. You write the date, the payee (who gets paid), the amount in numbers, the amount in words with cents as a fraction of 100, and your signature. The words are the legal amount if the two differ.
questions.question: Nora writes a check for $1,254.07. How should she write the amount in words on the check?

choices.text: One thousand two hundred fifty-four and 07/100 dollars
One thousand two hundred fifty-four and 7/10 dollars
Twelve hundred fifty-four point zero seven
One thousand two hundred forty-five and 07/100 dollars

questions.correct_answer: One thousand two hundred fifty-four and 07/100 dollars

misconceptions.C: Uses "point" instead of the cents fraction

questions.feedback: $1,254.07 is written "One thousand two hundred fifty-four and 07/100 dollars."

questions.section_skill: Choose and use payment methods safely: checks, electronic transfers, and payment apps
questions.intro: To deposit or cash a check made out to you, you "endorse" it by signing the back. Adding "For deposit only" (a restrictive endorsement) means the check can only be deposited, which protects it if it is lost. For mobile deposit, banks often require "For mobile deposit only" too.
questions.question: Ben receives a paycheck made out to him and wants to deposit it at an ATM. What should he write on the back?

choices.text: Nothing; endorsing a check is optional
His PIN, so the ATM can verify him
His account balance, so the bank can update it
His signature and "For deposit only"

questions.correct_answer: His signature and "For deposit only"

misconceptions.B: Writes sensitive data on a check
misconceptions.C: Thinks the balance goes on the check

questions.feedback: Signing with "For deposit only" endorses the check and limits it to being deposited.

questions.section_skill: Choose and use payment methods safely: checks, electronic transfers, and payment apps
questions.intro: Peer-to-peer (P2P) payment apps move money quickly between people. Money you send yourself, even when tricked, is usually treated as authorized and is often hard to get back. Federal error protections are strongest for transfers you did not authorize, such as when someone takes over your account. Use P2P apps mainly with people you know and trust.
questions.question: Mia sends $60 through a payment app to someone selling concert tickets online. The tickets never arrive. Which statement is most accurate about getting the payment back?

choices.text: The app must refund every payment that goes wrong
Her bank will reverse the payment automatically within one business day
The money is protected exactly like a stolen-card charge
Payments she authorized are often hard or impossible to reverse

questions.correct_answer: Payments she authorized are often hard or impossible to reverse

misconceptions.C: Confuses an authorized payment with an unauthorized transfer

questions.feedback: Because Mia authorized the payment, getting it back depends largely on the app's or bank's policies; she should report it quickly anyway.

questions.section_skill: Choose and use payment methods safely: checks, electronic transfers, and payment apps
questions.intro: Mobile check deposit lets you photograph a signed check in your bank's app. The bank may hold part of the money for a few days. Keep the paper check until the deposit is final, then destroy it securely so it cannot be deposited twice or misused.
questions.question: After depositing a check with his phone, what should Kai do with the paper check?

choices.text: Keep it until the deposit is final, then destroy it
Deposit the same check again at the bank to be safe
Throw it in the trash right after taking the photo
Give it back to the person who wrote it

questions.correct_answer: Keep it until the deposit is final, then destroy it

misconceptions.C: Discards it before the deposit is confirmed

questions.feedback: Keep it until the funds are final in case the bank needs it, then shred it.

questions.section_skill: Choose and use payment methods safely: checks, electronic transfers, and payment apps
questions.question: Zara's landlord asks for rent in a way that leaves a record of payment. Which method fits BEST?

choices.text: A check or an electronic transfer from her bank account
Cash handed over without a receipt
A gift card code sent by text
A wire transfer to an account number she has never verified

questions.correct_answer: A check or an electronic transfer from her bank account
questions.feedback: Checks and bank transfers leave records Zara can use as proof of payment.

questions.intro: Common ways to pay: cash; debit cards and checks (from your account); electronic transfers such as online bill pay and automatic payments (from your account, electronically); credit cards (borrowed money); and prepaid or gift cards (money loaded in advance).
questions.question: Which payment method moves money directly from your bank account electronically on a date you set?

choices.text: A paper check that the store mails to you each month
A credit card
A store gift card
An online bill payment or automatic transfer

questions.correct_answer: An online bill payment or automatic transfer

misconceptions.B: Confuses borrowing with paying from your account
misconceptions.C: Confuses prepaid value with an account payment

questions.feedback: Online bill pay and automatic payments take money from your account electronically.

questions.intro: A payment record proves you paid. Bank statements, cleared checks, and confirmation numbers are records. Cash leaves no record unless you get a receipt.
questions.question: Which method gives the LEAST proof that you paid?

choices.text: A check that the bank later shows as cleared
A debit card purchase listed on the statement
An online bill payment with a confirmation number
Cash with no receipt

questions.correct_answer: Cash with no receipt

misconceptions.A: A cleared check is a record

questions.feedback: Cash without a receipt leaves no proof of payment.

questions.intro: A prepaid or gift card holds a set amount of money. Each purchase is subtracted until the card reaches $0.
questions.question: A gift card loaded with $50 is used to buy a $12 item. What is left on the card?

misconceptions.C: Thinks the card balance does not change
misconceptions.A: Confuses the price with what is left

questions.question: Who is the "payee" on a check?

choices.text: The person or business that receives the money
The account holder who signs and writes the check
The bank that prints the check
The cashier who accepts the check

questions.correct_answer: The person or business that receives the money

misconceptions.B: Confuses payee with the account holder

questions.feedback: The payee is named on the "Pay to the order of" line.

questions.question: Which situation makes a payment app MOST risky to use?

choices.text: Paying a stranger online before receiving the item
Splitting a dinner bill with a close friend
Paying a family member back for groceries
Sending rent money to a roommate you have lived with for a year

questions.correct_answer: Paying a stranger online before receiving the item
questions.feedback: Paying strangers in advance is how many P2P scams work, because payments are hard to reverse.

questions.section_skill: Wires, ACH transfers, and official checks
questions.intro: A wire transfer moves money between banks quickly, often the same day, and is generally final once sent. ACH transfers (used for direct deposit and online bill pay) move money between bank accounts more slowly and have some ways to return errors. Scammers often ask for wires because they are fast and hard to reverse.
questions.question: Which payment is generally the hardest to reverse once sent?

choices.text: A credit card purchase
A check that has not been cashed yet
A debit card purchase you did not authorize
A wire transfer

questions.correct_answer: A wire transfer

misconceptions.B: A stop payment may be possible

questions.feedback: Wires are fast and generally final, which is why scammers prefer them.

questions.section_skill: Wires, ACH transfers, and official checks
questions.intro: A cashier's check is drawn on the bank's own funds, so a real one is very reliable. But fake cashier's checks are common. The bank may make the money available before discovering the check is fake; when it bounces, you owe the bank the full amount.
questions.question: A buyer sends Liam a cashier's check for $1,500 for a $500 phone and asks him to wire back the extra $1,000. What is most likely happening?

choices.text: A fake-check scam
A generous buyer making an honest mistake
A normal practice for cashier's checks
A bank error that the bank will cover

questions.correct_answer: A fake-check scam

misconceptions.B: Ignores the classic overpayment scam pattern
misconceptions.D: Thinks the bank absorbs fraud losses

questions.feedback: Overpayment with a request to send money back is a classic fake-check scam. Liam would owe the bank when the check bounces.

questions.section_skill: Wires, ACH transfers, and official checks
questions.intro: The ACH (Automated Clearing House) network moves money electronically between bank accounts in batches. It is cheaper and slower than a wire transfer.
questions.question: Which is a typical use of an ACH transfer?

choices.text: Buying groceries with cash
Paying a bill with a paper money order bought at a store
Swiping a credit card at a store
An employer's direct deposit of paychecks

questions.correct_answer: An employer's direct deposit of paychecks
questions.feedback: Direct deposit and many automatic bill payments use the ACH network.

questions.section_skill: Wires, ACH transfers, and official checks
questions.intro: Criminals hack or fake emails and send new "updated" wire instructions so money goes to their account. Because wires are hard to reverse, verify instructions through a trusted phone number, not one in the suspicious email.
questions.question: Before wiring money for a home or apartment deposit, what is the safest step?

choices.text: Use the instructions in the most recent email, even if they changed
Wire the money quickly so you do not lose the apartment
Ask the sender to text you the account number again
Call a phone number you already know is real to confirm the instructions

questions.correct_answer: Call a phone number you already know is real to confirm the instructions

misconceptions.C: Uses the same possibly hacked channel

questions.feedback: Independent verification defeats changed-instructions scams.

questions.section_skill: Wires, ACH transfers, and official checks
questions.intro: Until a check is paid by your bank, you can ask the bank not to pay it. Banks usually charge a fee for this service, and it does not work on a check that has already cleared.
questions.question: Ruth wrote a check and then learned it was lost in the mail before it was cashed. What service could stop it?

choices.text: A stop payment order through her bank
A wire recall, which works on all checks
Reporting the check to the IRS
Writing a second check for the same amount

questions.correct_answer: A stop payment order through her bank
questions.feedback: A stop payment order tells the bank not to pay that check, if it has not already cleared.

questions.intro: A common scam claims you received money "by mistake" and asks you to send it back. Sometimes the original payment was made with stolen information and is later reversed, leaving you with the loss. Verify inside your own app or bank, never through a link or message.
questions.question: Someone texts Ava: "I sent you $200 by mistake — please send it back!" Her app shows no new money in her account. What should she do?

choices.text: Check her own account directly and send nothing
Send $200 back right away to be polite
Reply with her bank login so they can fix it
Send $100 as a compromise

questions.correct_answer: Check her own account directly and send nothing

misconceptions.D: Still sends money to a scammer

questions.feedback: Without verified money in her own account, there is nothing to return. Even if money did arrive, contact the app's support rather than sending money.

questions.question: Which setting adds the most protection to a payment app?

choices.text: Sharing your login with a parent and a friend so they can watch for fraud
Using the same password as your email
Turning off notifications
Multi-factor authentication and a passcode on the app

Interest is paid only after payday

questions.feedback: Scheduling right after pay arrives avoids overdrafts and protects savings from spending.

Put the repair on a credit card and never pay it off
Skip the repair and drive an unsafe car
Stop saving forever because savings got used

questions.correct_answer: Use savings, then rebuild them over the next months
questions.feedback: Savings exist for needs like this; rebuilding keeps the habit.

questions.intro: The envelope method sets a fixed amount for each spending category. When a category runs out, spending in it stops. Many apps copy this idea digitally.
questions.question: In the envelope method, cash for each category goes in its own envelope. What happens when the "eating out" envelope is empty?

A credit card covers the extra
The envelope refills automatically
Eating out stops until the next budget period

questions.correct_answer: Eating out stops until the next budget period
questions.feedback: The method works by stopping spending when a category's money is used up.

Which method plans to spend EVERY dollar of income on a purpose?

choices.text: A zero-based budget
Spending freely and checking the balance
Saving whatever is left at month end
Paying only the minimums on all bills

questions.correct_answer: A zero-based budget
questions.feedback: Zero-based budgets assign every dollar.

questions.question: Which situation shows a budget that needs revising?

choices.text: One unusual month with a holiday gift
Spending matches the plan
A surplus that is saved
Spending is over budget in the same categories every month

questions.feedback: Repeated overspending means the plan is unrealistic and should be changed.

questions.question: Sam's grocery budget is $300, but he has spent $360, $350, and $370 in the last three months. What is the most realistic revised budget, based on his average?
questions.feedback: Average: ($360 + $350 + $370) ÷ 3 = $360. He should budget about $360 or find real ways to spend less.

Leave it unassigned so it is spent on something later

questions.section_skill: Plan for periodic and irregular expenses with monthly set-asides
questions.intro: Some expenses come once or twice a year: car registration, insurance premiums, school fees, gifts. A sinking fund saves a little each month for a known future expense, so the full amount is ready when it is due. Monthly amount = total ÷ months until due.
questions.question: Cara's car registration costs $180 once a year. How much should she set aside each month so the money is ready?

misconceptions.D: Plans to pay the whole amount in one month

questions.feedback: $180 ÷ 12 = $15 per month.

questions.section_skill: Plan for periodic and irregular expenses with monthly set-asides
questions.intro: A sinking fund is for a KNOWN future cost with a known date. An emergency fund is for UNKNOWN surprises, such as a job loss or a sudden repair.
questions.question: Which is a sinking fund?

choices.text: Saving $50 a month for car insurance due every six months
Money spent on groceries each week of the month, as needed
An emergency fund for surprises you cannot predict
A loan used to pay a bill that is already past due

questions.correct_answer: Saving $50 a month for car insurance due every six months
questions.feedback: Saving monthly for a known, scheduled bill is a sinking fund.

questions.section_skill: Plan for periodic and irregular expenses with monthly set-asides
questions.question: Cara's yearly irregular costs: registration $180, car insurance $960, and holiday gifts $300. How much should she set aside each month in total?

questions.section_skill: Plan for periodic and irregular expenses with monthly set-asides
questions.intro: When the due date is less than a year away, divide by the months remaining, not by 12.
questions.question: It is March. Holiday gifts ($600) will be bought in November, 8 months away. How much should Ben save each month?

misconceptions.D: Saves it all in one month

questions.feedback: $600 ÷ 8 = $75 per month.

questions.section_skill: Plan for periodic and irregular expenses with monthly set-asides
questions.question: Why do budgets that ignore irregular expenses often fail?

choices.text: Irregular expenses are illegal to budget for
Irregular expenses are always paid by employers
Banks automatically pay irregular bills for free when they come
Large, predictable bills arrive with no money set aside

questions.correct_answer: Large, predictable bills arrive with no money set aside
questions.feedback: Spreading known costs across months prevents "surprise" bills that were predictable.

questions.intro: To turn a yearly amount into a monthly amount, divide by 12. To turn a monthly amount into a yearly amount, multiply by 12.
questions.question: A yearly fee is $240. What is the monthly equivalent?
A $35 monthly subscription costs how much per year?

questions.intro: For a bill due every few months, divide by the number of months between bills.
questions.question: A bill of $300 is due every 6 months. How much is that per month?
questions.feedback: $300 ÷ 6 = $50 per month.

questions.question: Which expense is MOST likely to be paid once a year?

choices.text: A weekly grocery trip
A monthly phone bill for service
A daily bus fare
A car registration renewal

questions.correct_answer: A car registration renewal
questions.feedback: Registrations, many insurance policies, and some memberships are yearly.

questions.question: A quarterly bill is due every 3 months. How many times a year is it paid?

misconceptions.B: Confuses months between bills with bills per year

questions.feedback: 12 months ÷ 3 = 4 payments per year.

questions.intro: When income varies (tips, commissions, gig work, seasonal jobs), budgeting on a low but realistic month keeps needs covered. Extra income in good months goes to savings or a "buffer" that carries you through slow months.

misconceptions.B: Uses the average, which leaves no cushion in low months

questions.feedback: Planning on the lowest recent month ($1,500) keeps needs covered in slow months.

questions.section_skill: Use a decision process and recognize biases that lead to poor spending choices
questions.intro: Every spending choice has an opportunity cost: the next-best thing you give up. Thinking about what else money could do helps you choose deliberately rather than automatically.
questions.question: Kai has $200. He can buy a game console accessory or save toward a used bike. If he buys the accessory, what is the opportunity cost?

Nothing, because he still has the accessory
The sales tax on the accessory
The progress toward the bike that he gives up

questions.section_skill: Use a decision process and recognize biases that lead to poor spending choices
questions.intro: Anchoring is relying too much on the first number you see. A high "original" price can make a sale price feel cheap, even when it is not a good deal compared with other options.
questions.question: A sign says "Was $200, now $120!" Mia feels the $120 price is a great deal, even though similar items cost $100 elsewhere. Which bias is at work?

questions.section_skill: Use a decision process and recognize biases that lead to poor spending choices
questions.intro: A sunk cost is money already spent that cannot be recovered. The sunk cost fallacy is letting it drive a new decision. Good decisions compare the future benefits and costs of each option.

Opportunity cost bias
Anchoring
Comparison shopping

questions.section_skill: Use a decision process and recognize biases that lead to poor spending choices
questions.intro: Present bias is valuing what we want now much more than what we want later. Impulse buying feeds on it. Adding a delay, such as a 24-hour rule or removing saved cards, gives the planning part of the brain time to weigh in.
questions.question: Ana often buys things online late at night and regrets them. Which strategy targets this habit directly?

Turn on more shopping notifications
Shop only during sales events

questions.section_skill: Size, build, and use an emergency fund
questions.intro: An emergency fund is money saved for unexpected events: a lost job, a medical bill, a car repair. It helps you avoid high-cost borrowing when surprises happen. A common guideline is 3 to 6 months of essential expenses, built up gradually. Even a small fund helps.

Investing in stocks for the highest return
Unexpected costs such as a car repair or a job loss
Paying for holiday gifts each December

questions.feedback: Emergency funds cover unplanned needs; planned goals and investing belong elsewhere.

questions.intro: The "rollover" step: when one debt is paid off, its payment is added to the next target, so payments grow like a snowball.
questions.question: After Card B ($400) is paid off, Lee rolls its $40 minimum plus his $200 extra into the next debt. How much now goes to the next debt each month beyond its own minimum?

questions.intro: The interest saved by paying one debt instead of another is about the amount × the difference in rates.
questions.question: Two $1,000 debts: one at 25% APR, one at 5% APR. Paying the 25% debt first instead of the 5% debt avoids roughly how much interest per year on that $1,000?

questions.intro: A debt inventory, a list of every debt with its balance, rate, and minimum payment, is the starting point for any payoff plan.
questions.question: Which step should come BEFORE choosing a payoff method?

choices.text: Listing each debt's balance, rate, and minimum
Opening a new credit card
Skipping minimum payments on the smallest debts for a while
Closing all savings accounts

questions.correct_answer: Listing each debt's balance, rate, and minimum
questions.feedback: You cannot choose a target without knowing balances, rates, and minimums.

questions.intro: Debt consolidation combines several debts into one new loan, ideally at a lower rate. It can lower interest and simplify payments, but only if the new rate is lower and new debt is not added.
questions.question: Pia combines $6,000 of credit card debt at 23% APR into a personal loan at 11% interest with no other finance charges. About how much interest does this save in the first year (simple estimate on the full balance)?

questions.intro: Consolidation moves debt; it does not change spending habits.
questions.question: After consolidating, Pia keeps using her credit cards and builds new balances. What happens?

choices.text: The loan pays the new card debt automatically
Her rate on the cards drops to 11%
Her total debt goes down
She ends up with the loan AND new card debt

questions.correct_answer: She ends up with the loan AND new card debt
questions.feedback: Without changing spending, consolidation can lead to more total debt.

questions.intro: An origination fee is a one-time charge for making a loan, often a percent of the loan amount. It adds to the cost and should be included in comparisons.
questions.question: A consolidation loan has a 5% origination fee on $6,000. How much is the fee?

questions.intro: Debt relief companies that sell services by phone generally cannot charge fees until they actually settle or reduce a debt. Up-front fee demands are a warning sign.
questions.question: Which consolidation offer should raise suspicion?

choices.text: A credit union loan with a stated APR and no prepayment penalty
A bank personal loan with a clear fee schedule
A company that wants large fees up front to "settle" debts
A nonprofit credit counselor offering a free budget review

questions.correct_answer: A company that wants large fees up front to "settle" debts
questions.feedback: Up-front fees for debt settlement are a red flag.

questions.intro: Nonprofit credit counseling agencies can review your budget and debts and may offer debt management plans.
questions.question: Where can someone get free or low-cost help making a debt plan?

choices.text: A payday lender
An anonymous social media account offering tips
A rent-to-own store
A nonprofit credit counseling agency

questions.correct_answer: A nonprofit credit counseling agency
questions.feedback: Reputable nonprofit credit counselors help with budgets and debt plans.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Explain the consequences of missed payments and the rights of consumers with debt in collection
questions.intro: Consequences of a missed payment build over time. Right after the due date, the issuer can charge a late fee. Once a payment is 30 or more days past due, it can be reported to credit bureaus. Debts left unpaid for months can go to collectors or court.
questions.question: Ana misses a credit card payment by 10 days. Which consequence is MOST likely first?

choices.text: A fee for paying late
Immediate arrest
Her wages are garnished the next day
A 30-day late mark on her credit report

questions.correct_answer: A fee for paying late

misconceptions.D: A payment is not reported late until it is 30 or more days past due

questions.feedback: At 10 days late, a late fee is the likely consequence; credit reporting generally starts at 30+ days late.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Explain the consequences of missed payments and the rights of consumers with debt in collection
questions.intro: Under federal law, most negative items stay on credit reports for 7 years. Some bankruptcies can stay for up to 10 years. Positive information can stay longer.
questions.question: A 30-day late payment was reported in March 2020. Under the usual rule for negative items, about when should it drop off Ana's credit report?

choices.text: Around March 2021
Around March 2030
Around March 2027
Never; late payments stay forever

questions.correct_answer: Around March 2027

misconceptions.B: Uses the 10-year bankruptcy period for every item

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Explain the consequences of missed payments and the rights of consumers with debt in collection
questions.intro: The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act gives consumers rights: collectors must provide validation information about the debt, consumers can dispute it, and collectors may not harass, threaten, or lie.
questions.question: A debt collector calls about an old debt Sam does not recognize. What right does he have?

choices.text: To have the whole debt erased simply by asking for that
To make the collector pay him for the call
None; collectors can say anything
To dispute the debt and receive validation information

questions.correct_answer: To dispute the debt and receive validation information
questions.feedback: He can dispute the debt; the collector must provide information validating it.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Explain the consequences of missed payments and the rights of consumers with debt in collection
questions.intro: Collectors may not threaten arrest or legal action they cannot or do not intend to take.
questions.question: A collector threatens to have Rina arrested over a $400 credit card debt. What is true?

choices.text: This threat is illegal; debt is not a crime
She must pay immediately or go to jail
Collectors may say anything to get paid
Arrest is a normal step for unpaid debts over $300

questions.correct_answer: This threat is illegal; debt is not a crime
questions.feedback: Threatening arrest for ordinary debt is a prohibited practice. She can report it to the CFPB.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Explain the consequences of missed payments and the rights of consumers with debt in collection
questions.intro: Bankruptcy is a federal court process. Chapter 7 can discharge many debts, sometimes after selling some assets; Chapter 13 sets a repayment plan, usually over 3–5 years. Some debts, such as most student loans and child support, are hard or impossible to discharge.
questions.question: What is bankruptcy?

choices.text: A free way to cancel all debts with no consequences
A payment plan arranged by a debt collector
A court process to erase or reorganize debts
A credit score below 500

questions.correct_answer: A court process to erase or reorganize debts

misconceptions.B: Confuses bankruptcy with a repayment plan
misconceptions.D: Confuses a legal process with a credit rating

questions.feedback: Bankruptcy is a serious legal option of last resort with lasting credit effects.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Due dates, late fees, and minimum payments
questions.intro: A due date is the deadline for a payment. Paying after it can bring a late fee and, if very late, other consequences.
questions.question: A bill says "Due June 15." Ali pays on June 18. What usually happens?

choices.text: He may be charged a late fee
Nothing, because three days is close enough
The bill is cancelled
He earns interest

questions.correct_answer: He may be charged a late fee
questions.feedback: Paying after the due date can trigger a late fee.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Due dates, late fees, and minimum payments
questions.intro: The minimum payment is the smallest amount that keeps an account in good standing that month. It does not pay off the balance.
questions.question: A card's minimum payment is $35 on a $900 balance. If Ali pays $35, what happens to the rest?

choices.text: It is forgiven
It is paid by the card company
It must be paid separately in cash at a bank branch
It carries over and can be charged interest

questions.correct_answer: It carries over and can be charged interest
questions.feedback: The remaining $865 carries over, often with interest.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Due dates, late fees, and minimum payments
questions.question: Which habit best prevents missed payments?

choices.text: Paying only when reminded by a collector
Waiting for paper bills only
Autopay for at least the minimum
Paying whatever is left at month end

questions.correct_answer: Autopay for at least the minimum
questions.feedback: Autopay for at least the minimum, plus extra when possible, prevents late payments.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Due dates, late fees, and minimum payments
questions.intro: Compare a fee with the payment: fee ÷ payment × 100. Federal rules cap a credit card late fee at the amount of the minimum payment that was missed.
questions.question: A card charges a $20 late fee when a $25 minimum payment is missed. The fee equals what percent of the minimum payment?

misconceptions.A: Uses the fee as a percent

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Due dates, late fees, and minimum payments
questions.question: If you know you will miss a payment, what should you do first?

choices.text: Ignore all calls and letters until the problem passes
Open a new card to pay it
Contact the lender to ask about options
Change your phone number

questions.correct_answer: Contact the lender to ask about options
questions.feedback: Lenders may offer hardship plans or new due dates if contacted early.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.intro: Consumers can tell a debt collector in writing to stop contacting them. The collector may then contact them only to confirm or to say it will take a specific action, such as filing a lawsuit. The debt itself still exists.
questions.question: Sam wants a collector to stop calling. Under federal rules, what can he do?

choices.text: Nothing; calls cannot be stopped
Pay a fee to stop the calls
Ask his bank to block the debt from being collected
Ask in writing that it stop contacting him

questions.correct_answer: Ask in writing that it stop contacting him
questions.feedback: A written request stops most contact, though the debt remains and the collector may still sue.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.intro: After a collector first contacts you, it must send validation information. If you dispute the debt in writing within the validation period (generally 30 days), the collector must pause collection until it verifies the debt.
questions.question: Sam receives a debt validation notice on May 1 and believes the amount is wrong. By about when should he send a written dispute so the collector must verify the debt before continuing?

choices.text: By about May 31
By May 4
By about November 1
Any time, since there is no deadline

questions.correct_answer: By about May 31
questions.feedback: About 30 days from May 1 is May 31.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.intro: Collectors may contact you to collect, but federal law bans harassment, threats, false statements, and unfair practices.
questions.question: Which collector behavior is prohibited?

choices.text: Calling repeatedly to harass
Sending a letter with the amount owed
Calling during normal hours to ask for payment
Offering a payment plan

questions.correct_answer: Calling repeatedly to harass
questions.feedback: Harassment, such as repeated calls meant to annoy, is prohibited.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.intro: The CFPB and state attorneys general accept complaints about debt collection.
questions.question: Where can someone report a collector who breaks the rules?

choices.text: The collector's own sales and marketing team
A social media influencer
The CFPB or the state attorney general
The IRS

questions.correct_answer: The CFPB or the state attorney general
questions.feedback: The CFPB and state attorneys general handle these complaints.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.intro: A settlement is an agreement to pay less than the full balance. Get the terms in writing before paying, and keep proof of payment.
questions.question: A collector offers to settle a $2,000 debt for $1,200. What should Sam get before paying?

choices.text: Nothing; a phone promise is enough
A promise over the phone only
A new credit card from the collector
The settlement agreement in writing

questions.correct_answer: The settlement agreement in writing

misconceptions.B: Spoken promises are hard to prove

questions.feedback: A written agreement protects against later claims for the rest.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.intro: Most negative items can stay on a credit report for about 7 years. For a collection account, the period is measured from the original delinquency that led to it; selling the debt to a collector does not restart the clock.
questions.question: Sam's account first became delinquent 3 years ago and later went to collections. Under the usual 7-year rule, measured from that original delinquency, about how many more years will it typically stay on his credit report?

choices.text: About 4 years
7 years
10 years
0 years

questions.correct_answer: About 4 years

misconceptions.B: Restarts the clock when the debt goes to a collector

questions.feedback: About 7 − 3 = 4 more years (an approximation under the 7-year rule).

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.intro: The impact of old negative items fades over time, especially when new on-time payments build a better record.
questions.question: Which action usually helps a credit report recover over time?

choices.text: Opening many new cards at once
Ignoring all mail from creditors
Paying a company to erase accurate negatives
Making every new payment on time

questions.correct_answer: Making every new payment on time

misconceptions.C: Accurate information cannot be removed for a fee

questions.feedback: Recent on-time payments gradually outweigh older problems.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.intro: You can dispute inaccurate information for free. Accurate negative information generally can stay for the time the law allows. You have no right to demand its removal, and no paid service can guarantee it, although a creditor may sometimes choose to update or remove an item.
questions.question: A company promises to remove ACCURATE, current negative information from a credit report for $500. What should a consumer know?

choices.text: Paying more guarantees removal
It is the only way to fix credit
No one can legally force removal of accurate information
The credit bureaus require consumers to buy this service

questions.correct_answer: No one can legally force removal of accurate information
questions.feedback: Credit repair companies cannot legally force accurate items off a report; disputing errors is free.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.intro: A statute of limitations limits how long a creditor can sue over a debt. It varies by state, and in some states a payment can restart the clock.
questions.question: In some states, making a small payment on a very old debt can do what?

choices.text: Erase the debt entirely
Guarantee a perfect credit score
Make the debt illegal to collect from that point on
Restart the time limit for a lawsuit on that debt

questions.correct_answer: Restart the time limit for a lawsuit on that debt
questions.feedback: Before paying an old debt, learn your state's rules on the statute of limitations.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.intro: Chapter 13 bankruptcy reorganizes debts: a person with regular income repays creditors through a court-approved plan.
questions.question: Which statement about Chapter 13 bankruptcy is TRUE?

choices.text: It erases every debt instantly
It is the same as a debt management plan from a counselor
It sets a court-approved repayment plan, often 3–5 years
It has no effect on credit

questions.correct_answer: It sets a court-approved repayment plan, often 3–5 years
questions.feedback: Chapter 13 reorganizes debts into a repayment plan, usually 3–5 years.

questions.section_skill: Explain how a credit card works: credit limit, revolving balance, and grace period
questions.intro: A credit card lets you borrow up to a credit limit to make purchases. The card issuer pays the store, and you owe the issuer. Each month you get a statement and can pay the full balance or a smaller amount (at least the minimum). Any unpaid balance "revolves" to the next month, usually with interest.
questions.question: Leo uses a credit card to buy a $90 jacket. What happens to his money right away?

choices.text: Nothing yet; he now owes the card issuer $90
$90 leaves his checking account immediately, as with a debit card
The store waits to be paid until Leo pays his bill
The jacket is free if he pays the minimum each month

questions.correct_answer: Nothing yet; he now owes the card issuer $90
questions.feedback: The issuer paid the store; Leo now owes the issuer $90.

questions.section_skill: Explain how a credit card works: credit limit, revolving balance, and grace period
questions.intro: The credit limit is the most you can owe on the card at one time. Available credit = credit limit − current balance.
questions.question: Mia's card has a $1,500 credit limit and a $620 balance. How much more can she charge?

misconceptions.D: Adds the balance to the limit

questions.feedback: $1,500 − $620 = $880 of available credit.

questions.section_skill: Explain how a credit card works: credit limit, revolving balance, and grace period
questions.intro: Most cards offer a grace period on purchases: if you pay the full statement balance by the due date, you are not charged interest on those purchases. Grace periods usually do not apply to cash advances. The law requires statements to be sent at least 21 days before the due date. Carrying a balance usually ends the grace period until the card is paid in full again.
questions.question: Ben's card offers a grace period on purchases. He makes only purchases (no cash advances or balance transfers) and pays the full statement balance by the due date every month. How much interest does he pay on purchases?

choices.text: The full APR on every purchase
Half the APR, because he pays on time
$25 a month, the minimum payment

misconceptions.D: Confuses the minimum payment with interest

questions.feedback: With a purchase grace period and full, on-time payment, no purchase interest is charged.

questions.section_skill: Explain how a credit card works: credit limit, revolving balance, and grace period
questions.intro: Credit comes in two main forms. Installment credit (car loans, student loans) is one amount repaid in fixed payments. Revolving credit (credit cards, lines of credit) can be used again and again up to a limit, with payments that change with the balance.
questions.question: Which statement describes "revolving" credit?

choices.text: You borrow one fixed amount and repay it on a schedule
You can only use it once, then the account closes
The balance is paid automatically by the bank
You can borrow, repay, and borrow again up to a limit

questions.correct_answer: You can borrow, repay, and borrow again up to a limit
questions.feedback: Credit cards are revolving: available credit returns as you repay.

questions.section_skill: Explain how a credit card works: credit limit, revolving balance, and grace period
questions.intro: The Credit CARD Act says applicants under 21 must show independent income or assets enough to make the minimum payments, or have a cosigner or joint applicant who is at least 21 and able to pay, if the issuer allows that.
questions.question: Jada is 19, has no income, and has no savings or other assets of her own. She applies for a credit card. Under federal law, what does she need?

choices.text: A cosigner or joint applicant 21 or older
Only a school ID, because students get automatic approval
Nothing; anyone over 18 must be approved
A parent's permission slip signed at school

questions.correct_answer: A cosigner or joint applicant 21 or older
questions.feedback: With no independent income or assets, she needs a qualified cosigner or joint applicant 21 or older (where the issuer allows one).

questions.intro: A debit card takes money from your own account. A credit card borrows money you must repay.
questions.question: With a DEBIT card, where does the money come from?

choices.text: The cardholder's own bank account
A loan from the card issuer, repaid next month
The store's savings account
The government

questions.correct_answer: The cardholder's own bank account
questions.feedback: Debit spends money already in your account.

questions.intro: Every credit card purchase is borrowing. The amount is added to your card balance, which you owe the card issuer.
questions.question: With a CREDIT card, what does the cardholder create with each purchase?

choices.text: A deposit into savings
A gift from the store
A reduction in their bank balance right away
A debt owed to the card issuer

questions.correct_answer: A debt owed to the card issuer
questions.feedback: Each credit purchase adds to what you owe.

questions.intro: A credit limit is a borrowing maximum, not money you own.
questions.question: Sam's credit limit is $2,000. Does that mean he has $2,000 of his own money?

choices.text: Yes; the limit is deposited into his account
Yes, but only on weekends
No; it is the most he can borrow
No; it is the minimum he must spend

questions.correct_answer: No; it is the most he can borrow
questions.feedback: The limit is borrowing capacity that must be repaid.

questions.intro: Interest is charged on borrowed money that is not repaid on time.
questions.question: Which payment method can lead to paying INTEREST if the bill is not paid in full?

choices.text: A debit card
Cash
A credit card
A prepaid gift card

questions.correct_answer: A credit card

misconceptions.A: No interest; it spends your own money

questions.feedback: Unpaid credit card balances can be charged interest.

questions.intro: Federal law caps your liability for unauthorized credit card charges at $50. Debit card limits depend on how fast you report a problem.
questions.question: Which card typically has STRONGER federal protection against unauthorized charges?

choices.text: A debit card
A store gift card
A library card
A credit card

questions.correct_answer: A credit card
questions.feedback: Credit cards have a $50 cap; debit card protection depends on how quickly you report.

questions.section_skill: What is APR on a credit card?
questions.intro: A credit card's APR is its yearly interest rate. Interest for about a month ≈ balance × (APR ÷ 12). (Many cards actually figure interest daily.)
questions.question: A card has a 24% purchase APR. If Kai carries a $500 balance for a whole month, about how much interest is charged (monthly rate = APR ÷ 12)?

questions.section_skill: What is APR on a credit card?
questions.intro: Cards can have different APRs for purchases, cash advances, and balance transfers, plus a penalty APR that can apply after a late payment, often 60 days late for existing balances.
questions.question: A card lists several APRs: purchase APR 21.99%, cash advance APR 29.99%, penalty APR 29.99%. When does the PENALTY APR usually apply?

choices.text: After a serious late payment
On every purchase made on weekends
Only on balance transfers made in the first month
Never; it is only shown for decoration

questions.correct_answer: After a serious late payment
questions.feedback: The penalty APR applies after late payments, as described in the agreement.

questions.section_skill: What is APR on a credit card?
questions.intro: The best card depends on how you use it. If you keep a purchase grace period by always paying in full on time, the APR rarely matters, but fees do.
questions.question: Two cards, both with a grace period on purchases: Card A 18% APR, $0 annual fee; Card B 15% APR, $95 annual fee. Ana uses the card only for purchases and pays the full statement balance on time every month. Which costs her less?

choices.text: Card B, because 15% is lower than 18%
They cost the same
Card B, because annual fees are refunded
Card A, because she pays no interest

questions.correct_answer: Card A, because she pays no interest

misconceptions.A: Ignores that she pays no interest

questions.feedback: Paying in full on time means no purchase interest, so the $95 fee is the only cost difference.

questions.section_skill: What is APR on a credit card?
questions.intro: Under the Credit CARD Act, issuers generally must give 45 days' notice before a significant change such as a higher APR on new purchases.
questions.question: Maya's card issuer plans to raise the APR on new purchases starting July 1. Under the CARD Act, by about when must she receive notice?

choices.text: By June 24
By June 30
By about May 17
Notice is not required before the change

questions.correct_answer: By about May 17
questions.feedback: 45 days before July 1 is May 17.

questions.section_skill: What is APR on a credit card?
questions.intro: Daily interest = balance × (APR ÷ 365).
questions.question: A 24% APR card charges interest daily on a $500 balance. About what is the daily interest (APR ÷ 365)?

questions.intro: A cash advance means using your credit card to get cash (at an ATM or bank). It is borrowing. Cash advances usually have a fee, a higher APR, and no grace period: interest starts right away.
questions.question: A cash advance is…

choices.text: borrowing cash against your credit card
withdrawing your own savings with a debit card
a free bonus paid by the card issuer
a refund of a returned purchase

questions.correct_answer: borrowing cash against your credit card
questions.feedback: A cash advance is a loan of cash from your card issuer.

questions.intro: Cash advance fees are often the larger of a percent of the amount or a minimum dollar amount.
questions.question: Tom takes a $200 cash advance. The fee is 5% (minimum $10). What is the fee?
questions.feedback: 5% of $200 = $10, which equals the $10 minimum, so the fee is $10.

questions.intro: Interest on a cash advance starts the day it is taken. Interest ≈ amount × (APR ÷ 365) × days.
questions.question: A $400 cash advance has a 5% fee and a 29.99% APR with no grace period. About how much interest accrues in 30 days (daily rate = APR ÷ 365)?

questions.intro: The total cost of a cash advance includes both the fee and the interest.
questions.question: Tom's $400 cash advance cost a $20 fee plus about $9.86 of interest after 30 days. What was the total cost?
Which is usually a cheaper way to get $100 cash quickly than a credit card cash advance?

choices.text: Taking a cash advance on two cards instead of one
A payday loan
A title loan
Withdrawing from your own savings or checking

questions.correct_answer: Withdrawing from your own savings or checking
questions.feedback: Using your own money avoids fees and interest.

questions.section_skill: Read a credit card statement and decide how much to pay and when
questions.intro: A credit card statement lists the previous balance, payments, new purchases, fees, interest, the new (statement) balance, the minimum payment, and the due date. Paying the full statement balance by the due date avoids interest on purchases (the grace period).
questions.question:
Credit card statement (closing date May 20): Previous balance $640.00 | Payments −$640.00 | Purchases +$412.75 | Fees $0.00 | Interest charged $0.00 | New balance $412.75 (purchases only; no cash advances) | Minimum payment due $25.00 | Payment due date June 15 | Purchase APR 22.99% | Grace period on purchases: yes, when the statement balance is paid in full by the due date
How much must Rosa pay by June 15 to avoid ANY interest on these purchases?
questions.feedback: Paying the full new balance, $412.75, by June 15 keeps the grace period.

questions.section_skill: Read a credit card statement and decide how much to pay and when
questions.intro: The minimum payment due is the smallest amount that avoids a late fee that month. Paying only the minimum leaves the rest of the balance owed, and interest is charged on it.
questions.question:
Credit card statement (closing date May 20): Previous balance $640.00 | Payments −$640.00 | Purchases +$412.75 | Fees $0.00 | Interest charged $0.00 | New balance $412.75 (purchases only; no cash advances) | Minimum payment due $25.00 | Payment due date June 15 | Purchase APR 22.99% | Grace period on purchases: yes, when the statement balance is paid in full by the due date
What is the LEAST Rosa can pay by June 15 and keep her account in good standing?
questions.feedback: The minimum payment due is $25.00; paying only that leaves $387.75 to carry over with interest.

questions.section_skill: Read a credit card statement and decide how much to pay and when
questions.question:
Credit card statement (closing date May 20): Previous balance $640.00 | Payments −$640.00 | Purchases +$412.75 | Fees $0.00 | Interest charged $0.00 | New balance $412.75 (purchases only; no cash advances) | Minimum payment due $25.00 | Payment due date June 15 | Purchase APR 22.99% | Grace period on purchases: yes, when the statement balance is paid in full by the due date
If Rosa pays only the $25 minimum, what balance carries into next month before interest?
questions.feedback: $412.75 − $25.00 = $387.75, which will then be charged interest.

questions.section_skill: Read a credit card statement and decide how much to pay and when
questions.intro: When the previous statement balance was paid in full by its due date, new purchases usually get a grace period, so no purchase interest appears on the next statement.
questions.question:
Credit card statement (closing date May 20): Previous balance $640.00 | Payments −$640.00 | Purchases +$412.75 | Fees $0.00 | Interest charged $0.00 | New balance $412.75 (purchases only; no cash advances) | Minimum payment due $25.00 | Payment due date June 15 | Purchase APR 22.99% | Grace period on purchases: yes, when the statement balance is paid in full by the due date
The statement shows "Interest charged $0.00." Why?

choices.text: Paying the last balance in full kept the grace period
Her card has no interest rate at all
Interest is only charged in June
The card issuer forgot to add this month's interest charge

questions.correct_answer: Paying the last balance in full kept the grace period
questions.feedback: Paying the full $640 previous balance kept the grace period.

questions.section_skill: Read a credit card statement and decide how much to pay and when
questions.intro: Federal law requires statements to show how long it would take to pay off the balance making only minimum payments, and the total cost, compared with a payment that pays it off in 3 years.
questions.question: A statement's "minimum payment warning" says paying only the minimum will take 9 years and cost $2,100 in total on a $1,000 balance. What does this tell the cardholder?

choices.text: The minimum payment is always the best choice
The remaining balance will be forgiven after 9 years
The minimum route costs far more and takes longer
The interest rate will drop to 0%

Only whether the new card has an annual fee

questions.section_skill: Explain what credit reports contain, get free reports, and dispute errors
questions.intro: A credit report is a record of how you have used credit: accounts, balances, payment history, and some collections. Three nationwide credit bureaus (consumer reporting agencies) keep reports: Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion.
questions.question: Which company is one of the three nationwide credit bureaus?

choices.text: Experian
The Federal Reserve
The IRS
Visa

questions.correct_answer: Experian
questions.feedback: Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion are the three nationwide credit bureaus.

questions.section_skill: Explain what credit reports contain, get free reports, and dispute errors
questions.intro: Federal law gives you free credit reports. The official site is AnnualCreditReport.com, where free reports from all three bureaus are available (weekly, under a permanent program).
questions.question: Where can Jordan get free credit reports from all three bureaus?

choices.text: Any website that advertises "free credit score"
The bank where Jordan opened checking
The IRS website
AnnualCreditReport.com

questions.correct_answer: AnnualCreditReport.com
questions.feedback: AnnualCreditReport.com is the official free source.

questions.section_skill: Explain what credit reports contain, get free reports, and dispute errors
questions.intro: Credit reports show identifying information, credit accounts (cards, loans), balances, credit limits, payment history, inquiries, and certain collections. They do not include income, bank balances, race, religion, or medical details.
questions.question: Which item is generally on a credit report?

choices.text: Whether card payments were on time
Your income and salary
Your race or religion
Your bank account balances

questions.correct_answer: Whether card payments were on time
questions.feedback: Payment history on credit accounts is a core part of credit reports.

questions.section_skill: Explain what credit reports contain, get free reports, and dispute errors
questions.intro: If a report has an error, you can dispute it with the credit bureau (and the company that reported it). The bureau generally must investigate, usually within 30 days. An account you never opened can be a sign of identity theft.
questions.question: Jordan's report lists a credit card she never opened. What should she do?

choices.text: Ignore it, since reports are always correct
Pay off the card to make it go away
Dispute it and check for identity theft
Ignore it if her score still looks fine

questions.correct_answer: Dispute it and check for identity theft

misconceptions.B: Pays a debt that is not hers

questions.feedback: Disputing errors is free; an unknown account may mean identity theft.

questions.section_skill: Explain what credit reports contain, get free reports, and dispute errors
questions.intro: Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, only those with a "permissible purpose" can see your report: lenders, insurers, landlords, and employers (with your written permission), among others.
questions.question: Who may legally see Jordan's credit report?

choices.text: A lender reviewing her application
Any curious neighbor who wants to know
A classmate who asks
A social media follower

questions.correct_answer: A lender reviewing her application
questions.feedback: Lenders evaluating applications have a permissible purpose.

questions.intro: Your credit history shows how you have handled borrowing: which accounts you have, how much you owe, and whether you paid on time.
questions.question: What is a credit history?

choices.text: A list of every purchase a person has made with cash
A list of a person's bank account balances
A record of how a person has borrowed and repaid
A record of a person's income each year

questions.correct_answer: A record of how a person has borrowed and repaid

misconceptions.B: Confuses credit history with bank balances
misconceptions.D: Credit reports do not list income

questions.feedback: Credit history tracks borrowing and repayment.

questions.intro: Credit accounts such as loans and credit cards are reported to credit bureaus. Cash and debit purchases usually are not.
questions.question: Which activity adds to a person's credit history?

choices.text: Paying cash for groceries
Using a debit card
Saving money in a piggy bank
Repaying a car loan on time

questions.correct_answer: Repaying a car loan on time
questions.feedback: Loans and credit cards build credit history.

questions.intro: Past repayment behavior helps lenders estimate the risk that a borrower will not repay.
questions.question: Why do lenders look at credit history?

choices.text: To learn which stores a borrower likes best
To set the borrower's salary
To decide the borrower's taxes
To predict whether a borrower will repay

questions.correct_answer: To predict whether a borrower will repay
questions.feedback: Past repayment helps predict future repayment.

questions.intro: People with few or no credit accounts have "thin" files, which makes it harder for lenders to judge them.
questions.question: A student with no loans or cards applies for credit. What problem might she face?

choices.text: A "thin" credit file with little history to judge
Her report will show many late payments from the past
She will be approved for any amount
She has a perfect score by default

questions.correct_answer: A "thin" credit file with little history to judge
questions.feedback: No history makes approval harder, not easier.

questions.intro: Credit history can affect renting an apartment, insurance prices in many states, and some job applications (with written permission).
questions.question: Besides lenders, who else may check credit history (with permission when required)?

choices.text: Movie theaters
Grocery store cashiers at checkout
Landlords and insurers
Classmates

questions.correct_answer: Landlords and insurers
questions.feedback: Landlords and insurers may review credit information for permissible purposes.

questions.section_skill: Reading a credit report line by line
questions.intro: Credit report account lines show the creditor, limit or loan amount, balance, and payment status by month. Late payments are usually reported once they are 30 or more days past due.
questions.question: A report line shows: "Card A — limit $2,000 — balance $600 — status: 30 days late (March)". What does "30 days late" mean?

choices.text: The card was opened 30 days ago
The card has 30 days of interest-free time each month
The balance is $30
A payment was at least 30 days past due in March

questions.correct_answer: A payment was at least 30 days past due in March
questions.feedback: A 30-day late payment was reported for March.

questions.section_skill: Reading a credit report line by line
questions.intro: A hard inquiry happens when a lender checks your credit because you applied for credit; it can lower scores slightly for a short time. Soft inquiries, such as checking your own report or prescreened offers, do not affect scores.
questions.question: A report shows two "hard inquiries" from lenders this month. What caused them?

choices.text: Applications for new credit
Checking your own report
Receiving a preapproved offer in the mail
Paying a bill on time

questions.correct_answer: Applications for new credit
questions.feedback: Hard inquiries come from credit applications.

questions.section_skill: Reading a credit report line by line
questions.intro: Soft inquiries, including checking your own credit, do not affect credit scores.
questions.question: Which inquiry does NOT affect a credit score?

choices.text: Applying for a car loan
Applying for a credit card
Checking your own credit report
Applying for a private student loan

questions.correct_answer: Checking your own credit report
questions.feedback: Checking your own credit is a soft inquiry with no score impact.

questions.section_skill: Reading a credit report line by line
questions.intro: Paying a collection usually updates its status to "paid," but the record can remain for the reporting period allowed by law.
questions.question: A report shows a collection account that Ana paid in full 2 years ago. What should it show now?

choices.text: The collection, updated to show it was paid
Nothing; paid collections vanish immediately
A new unpaid collection
A higher balance

questions.correct_answer: The collection, updated to show it was paid
questions.feedback: It should be updated as paid; it may remain on the report for the allowed time.

questions.section_skill: Reading a credit report line by line
questions.intro: Lenders choose which bureaus to report to, and reporting dates differ, so the three reports may not match exactly.
questions.question: Ana reviews her reports from all three bureaus. Why might they differ?

choices.text: One of them must be fake
Bureaus copy each other's reports exactly every day
Each bureau uses a different person's data
Not every lender reports to every bureau

questions.correct_answer: Not every lender reports to every bureau

misconceptions.B: Assumes the three bureaus share one file
misconceptions.C: Confuses reporting gaps with mixed files

questions.feedback: Different reporting leads to differences; check all three.

questions.section_skill: Freezes, fraud alerts, and identity protection
questions.intro: A credit freeze (security freeze) restricts access to your credit report, so identity thieves cannot easily open new accounts in your name. Freezes are free at each bureau, and you can lift them temporarily when you apply for credit.
questions.question: What does a credit freeze do?

choices.text: It lowers your credit score
It closes your existing cards
It blocks most new lenders from seeing your report
It stops you from using your own debit card or checks

questions.correct_answer: It blocks most new lenders from seeing your report

misconceptions.B: Confuses freezing a report with closing accounts
misconceptions.D: Confuses a credit freeze with freezing a bank account

questions.feedback: A freeze blocks most new-credit checks without affecting your score or existing accounts.

questions.section_skill: Freezes, fraud alerts, and identity protection
questions.intro: Since 2018, federal law has required the nationwide credit bureaus to place and lift credit freezes for free.
questions.question: How much does it cost to place a credit freeze at a nationwide bureau?

choices.text: $10 per bureau each year
$100 one time
A fee of 1% of your total credit limit
Nothing; freezes are free by law

questions.correct_answer: Nothing; freezes are free by law
questions.feedback: Freezes are free at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion.

questions.section_skill: Freezes, fraud alerts, and identity protection
questions.intro: You can lift a freeze temporarily for a specific time or lender, then it returns.

choices.text: Lift the freeze for a short time
Delete her credit history
Apply under a friend's name
Nothing; lenders can see frozen reports

questions.correct_answer: Lift the freeze for a short time
questions.feedback: A temporary lift lets the lender check her credit.

questions.section_skill: Freezes, fraud alerts, and identity protection
questions.intro: A fraud alert asks lenders to take extra steps to verify your identity before opening credit. A credit freeze blocks most access to your report.
questions.question: How is a fraud alert different from a credit freeze?

choices.text: An alert closes your existing accounts
A freeze costs money; an alert is free
An alert asks for ID checks; a freeze blocks access
They are identical; both close your current accounts

questions.correct_answer: An alert asks for ID checks; a freeze blocks access
questions.feedback: Alerts add verification; freezes restrict access.

questions.section_skill: Freezes, fraud alerts, and identity protection
questions.question: Which teen habit best protects future credit?

choices.text: Posting a full birth date and address online
Sharing passwords with friends
Using the same password everywhere
Keeping a Social Security number private

questions.correct_answer: Keeping a Social Security number private
questions.feedback: Protecting your SSN and personal data prevents thieves from opening accounts in your name.

questions.section_skill: Explain the factors that affect credit scores and how scores affect borrowing costs
questions.intro: A credit score is a number (often 300–850) that summarizes credit risk based on a credit report. FICO's general weights: payment history about 35%, amounts owed about 30%, length of credit history about 15%, new credit about 10%, and credit mix about 10%. Other scoring models exist.
questions.question: In the widely used FICO model, which factor has the LARGEST weight?

choices.text: Payment history (about 35%)
Credit mix (about 10%)
New credit (about 10%)
Length of credit history (about 15%)

questions.correct_answer: Payment history (about 35%)
questions.feedback: Paying on time matters most.

questions.section_skill: Explain the factors that affect credit scores and how scores affect borrowing costs
questions.intro: Credit scores affect the interest rates lenders offer. A higher score usually means a lower rate, which lowers monthly payments and total cost.
questions.question: Two applicants want a $20,000, 5-year car loan. Applicant A (strong credit) is offered 6% APR, with a $386.66 payment; Applicant B is offered 12% APR, with a $444.89 payment. How much more does B pay over 5 years?

questions.section_skill: Explain the factors that affect credit scores and how scores affect borrowing costs
questions.intro: Scores reward on-time payments and low balances compared with limits, and can drop with late payments, high balances, and many new applications.
questions.question: Which action is MOST likely to raise a credit score over time?

choices.text: Opening several new cards in one month
Maxing out a credit card
Paying every bill on time
Closing your oldest account

questions.correct_answer: Paying every bill on time
questions.feedback: Consistent on-time payments are the strongest positive factor.

questions.section_skill: Explain the factors that affect credit scores and how scores affect borrowing costs
questions.intro: Credit scores use only information in credit reports. Income, employment, savings, age, race, and where you live are not part of the score.

choices.text: Ben's is much higher
Ana's is higher because she borrows more of her income
They are about the same
Ben's is lower because higher earners spend more

questions.correct_answer: They are about the same

misconceptions.A: Believes income is part of the score

questions.feedback: Income is not in credit reports, so identical reports give about the same score (lenders may still ask about income).

questions.section_skill: Explain the factors that affect credit scores and how scores affect borrowing costs
questions.question: Ivy's FICO score is 780; Max's is 580. Which statement is MOST accurate?

choices.text: Max will pay lower rates, since lower is better
Both will get identical offers
Scores do not affect borrowing
Max will likely face higher rates or denials

questions.feedback: On the 300–850 scale, higher scores indicate lower risk and usually get better terms.

Amounts owed
Credit mix
Length of credit history

misconceptions.C: Nothing says their account types differ

questions.intro: Landlords often review credit reports or scores because past bill-paying predicts rent payment.

choices.text: To predict whether she will pay rent on time
To see her school grades
To check her medical history and recent doctor visits
To learn her income

questions.correct_answer: To predict whether she will pay rent on time
questions.feedback: Credit history helps landlords predict on-time rent.

questions.intro: Many insurers use credit-based insurance scores to help set prices, where state law allows.

choices.text: They pay lower premiums
They cannot buy insurance
They may pay higher premiums
Their driving record is ignored

questions.correct_answer: They may pay higher premiums
questions.feedback: Weaker credit can raise premiums in states that allow this.

questions.question: An employer wants to check Tia's credit report for a job. What must happen first?

choices.text: Nothing; employers can check anyone
Tia must pay a fee
The employer must pay Tia's credit card bill
Tia must give written permission

questions.correct_answer: Tia must give written permission
questions.feedback: Written permission is required for employment checks.

questions.intro: Over long loans, a small rate difference adds up: extra cost = monthly difference × number of payments.

Scores are updated only once a year
Scores are the same at every bureau

Fact: only on weekends
Myth: your own check is a soft inquiry
Fact: each check lowers your score by about 50 points

choices.text: Fact: interest payments raise scores
Myth: paying in full still shows on-time use

Fact: scores are a percent of income
Myth: income is not in credit reports

Fact: closed cards are deleted immediately

Myth: they usually count as one inquiry
