questions.section_skill: Build a credit history with low utilization, on-time payments, and starter credit products

questions.section_skill: Credit-builder loans and secured cards in detail
questions.intro: With a credit-builder loan, the lender holds the loan amount in an account while you make payments. Payments are reported to bureaus, and you receive the money at the end. The cost is the interest and fees.
questions.question: A credit-builder loan of $600 is held in a savings account while Ana makes 12 payments of $52. What does she receive at the end, and what did it cost?
questions.feedback: 12 × $52 = $624 paid; she receives $600; cost $24.

questions.section_skill: Credit-builder loans and secured cards in detail
questions.intro: A secured card works like a regular credit card for utilization: the balance reported to the credit bureaus (usually the statement balance) ÷ the credit limit.

questions.question: A high-yield ("junk") bond pays 8%, while an investment-grade bond pays 5%. Why the difference?

choices.text: The high-yield issuer is more likely to default
High-yield bonds are insured by the federal government
Investment-grade bonds have longer maturities, always
The difference is random

questions.correct_answer: The high-yield issuer is more likely to default

misconceptions.B: Believes higher yield comes with a guarantee
misconceptions.C: Attributes the gap only to maturity
misconceptions.D: Misses the link between risk and yield

questions.feedback: Higher yield compensates for higher default risk.

questions.set_title: Bonds: lending to governments and companies
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Bond funds pool money to buy many bonds. Owning many issuers spreads credit risk (a fund of hundreds of Treasuries, by contrast, has one issuer). Fund prices still change with interest rates.
questions.question: A bond fund holds bonds from hundreds of different companies and governments. What is one advantage over buying one bond?

choices.text: It can never lose value
It always pays the same fixed income each year
It is FDIC insured
Default risk is spread across many issuers

questions.correct_answer: Default risk is spread across many issuers

misconceptions.B: Confuses a fund with a single bond

questions.feedback: Owning many issuers spreads credit risk, though fund prices still move with rates.

questions.set_title: Bonds: lending to governments and companies
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: At maturity, a bond repays its face value, no matter what it was bought for. The last interest payment is usually paid at the same time, separately from the principal.
questions.question: A 2% bond with a $1,000 face value is selling for $900. If held to maturity with no default, how much PRINCIPAL is repaid at maturity (not counting the final interest payment)?

misconceptions.B: Adds one year of interest to the price
misconceptions.D: Adds the final interest payment to principal

questions.feedback: At maturity the issuer repays the full $1,000 face value as principal.

questions.set_title: Bonds: lending to governments and companies
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Gain on price = amount received at maturity − price paid.
questions.question: Bought at $900 and repaid at $1,000 at maturity, what is the gain on price alone?
questions.feedback: $1,000 − $900 = $100, plus coupon interest along the way.

questions.set_title: Bonds: lending to governments and companies
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Longer-term bonds lock in their coupon longer, so their prices are more sensitive to rate changes.
questions.question: Which bond's price usually changes MORE when interest rates change?

choices.text: A 3-month Treasury bill
A 30-year bond
A 1-year note
Neither; maturity does not matter

questions.correct_answer: A 30-year bond
questions.feedback: Longer maturities mean more interest rate risk.

questions.set_title: Bonds: lending to governments and companies
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Existing bond prices move opposite to interest rates.
questions.question: If interest rates FALL, what usually happens to the prices of existing bonds?

choices.text: They fall
They rise
They stay the same
They are cancelled

questions.correct_answer: They rise
questions.feedback: Older bonds with higher coupons become more valuable when rates fall.

questions.set_title: Bonds: lending to governments and companies
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Bond prices before maturity change with interest rates; holders who wait for maturity receive face value (if the issuer pays).
questions.question: Which investor is MOST affected by bond price swings before maturity?

choices.text: One who holds the bond to maturity
One who never bought a bond
One who must sell the bond early
One who only owns savings

questions.correct_answer: One who must sell the bond early
questions.feedback: Selling before maturity exposes you to the current market price.

questions.set_title: Mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Compare mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds and explain how they are priced
questions.intro: A mutual fund pools money from many investors to buy a collection (portfolio) of stocks, bonds, or other securities, managed by professionals. Each investor owns shares of the fund. Mutual fund shares are bought and sold once a day at the net asset value (NAV) calculated after the market closes.
questions.question: What is a mutual fund?

choices.text: A pool of investors' money that buys many securities
A single company's stock sold at a discount
An FDIC-insured savings product at a bank
A loan that a group of friends makes together to one person

questions.correct_answer: A pool of investors' money that buys many securities

misconceptions.B: Confuses a fund with one stock

questions.feedback: A mutual fund pools money to buy many securities.

questions.set_title: Mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Compare mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds and explain how they are priced
questions.intro: An ETF also holds a basket of securities, but its shares trade on stock exchanges throughout the day at market prices, like stocks. Traditional mutual funds trade once a day at NAV.
questions.question: How is an ETF (exchange-traded fund) different from a traditional mutual fund?

choices.text: ETFs can hold only one stock at a time
ETFs are insured by the FDIC
ETFs are bought only once a year at one fixed price
ETF shares trade on an exchange throughout the day

questions.correct_answer: ETF shares trade on an exchange throughout the day
questions.feedback: ETFs trade all day like stocks; mutual funds price once a day.

questions.set_title: Mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Compare mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds and explain how they are priced
questions.intro: An index is a list that measures part of the market; the S&P 500 tracks about 500 large U.S. companies. An index fund (a mutual fund or ETF) holds the securities in an index to match its performance, not to beat it. Index funds usually have low costs.
questions.question: What does an S&P 500 index fund try to do?

choices.text: Beat the S&P 500 by picking winning stocks each week
Guarantee a 5% return every year
Hold only the 5 largest companies
Match the performance of the S&P 500 index

questions.correct_answer: Match the performance of the S&P 500 index
questions.feedback: Index funds aim to match an index, typically at low cost.

questions.set_title: Mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Compare mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds and explain how they are priced
questions.intro: Net asset value per share = (total assets − total liabilities) ÷ shares outstanding.
questions.question: A fund has $50,000,000 in assets, $500,000 in liabilities, and 2,000,000 shares outstanding. What is its NAV per share?

questions.set_title: Mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Compare mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds and explain how they are priced
questions.question: Which statement about index funds is TRUE?

choices.text: They are guaranteed never to lose money
They are FDIC insured up to $250,000
They can lose value when the market falls
They always beat every other type of fund

questions.correct_answer: They can lose value when the market falls
questions.feedback: Index funds track the market, including its declines.

questions.set_title: Mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Pooling means combining money from many people. Each person owns a share equal to their part of the pool.
questions.question: Ten friends each put in $20 to buy a $200 gift together. What fraction of the gift does each friend "own"?

questions.set_title: Mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: In a fund, each holding is part of the whole, so a holding's drop affects the fund in proportion to its weight.
questions.question: A fund holds 400 stocks in equal amounts, so each is 0.25% of the fund. If one stock falls 50% and the others do not change, why does the fund fall only a little?

choices.text: The fund refunds the loss
That stock is only a small part of the fund
Funds sell any stock before it falls
The other 399 stocks in it must all rise by 50%

questions.correct_answer: That stock is only a small part of the fund

misconceptions.C: Believes managers can always avoid drops

questions.feedback: 0.25% × 50% ≈ 0.125%: one small slice moves the fund only a little.

questions.set_title: Mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.question: Who manages a mutual fund's investments?

choices.text: Each investor votes on every trade
The FDIC
Professional fund managers
The stock exchange

questions.correct_answer: Professional fund managers
questions.feedback: Funds are managed by professionals, for a fee.

questions.set_title: Mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: A fund share represents a proportional slice of everything the fund holds.
questions.question: Owning one share of a fund that holds 500 companies gives you…

choices.text: full ownership of one company
a tiny piece of all 500 companies
a loan to the fund manager, repaid later
a bank deposit

questions.correct_answer: a tiny piece of all 500 companies
questions.feedback: A fund share is a slice of everything the fund holds.

questions.set_title: Mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: A broad index fund holds many companies, so even a small purchase spreads money widely. Narrow funds (one sector, or leveraged funds) do not give the same diversification.
questions.question: Which choice is a BENEFIT of broad index funds for beginning investors?

choices.text: Instant diversification with a small amount
No risk of loss
Guaranteed returns
No fees ever

questions.correct_answer: Instant diversification with a small amount
questions.feedback: Broad funds give wide diversification even for small investments.

questions.set_title: Mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Active funds try to beat the market by choosing investments; they usually cost more. Passive (index) funds try to match the market at low cost.
questions.question: An actively managed fund charges 0.80% a year; an index fund tracking a similar market charges 0.05%. On $10,000, how much more does the active fund cost per year?

questions.set_title: Mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Net return ≈ gross return − expense ratio.
questions.question: An active fund returns 7.5% before its 0.80% expense ratio; the index fund returns 7.0% before its 0.05% ratio. Which has the higher return after expenses?

choices.text: The active fund: 7.5% vs 7.0%
They are equal at 7.0%
The active fund: 6.95% vs 6.70%
The index fund: 6.95% vs 6.70%

questions.correct_answer: The index fund: 6.95% vs 6.70%

questions.set_title: Mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Passive investing aims to match the market's return by owning the whole index, rather than predicting which stocks will do best.
questions.question: What does "passive" investing mean?

choices.text: Holding an index fund instead of trying to pick winners
Never checking your account again
Investing only in savings accounts
Letting a friend choose your stocks

questions.correct_answer: Holding an index fund instead of trying to pick winners
questions.feedback: Passive investing tracks a market index.

questions.set_title: Mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Trading inside a fund creates costs and, in taxable accounts, can create capital gains distributions.
questions.question: A fund's "turnover" is high, meaning it trades often. Why can that matter?

choices.text: High turnover guarantees higher returns
Frequent trading can raise costs and taxes
Turnover has no effect at all on what investors pay
Turnover is a type of insurance

questions.correct_answer: Frequent trading can raise costs and taxes
questions.feedback: Frequent trading adds hidden costs and possible tax bills.

questions.set_title: Mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Every mutual fund and ETF publishes a prospectus (and a shorter summary) describing its objectives, strategy, risks, and costs.
questions.question: Which document gives a fund's goals, risks, fees, and past performance?

choices.text: The fund's quarterly advertisement
Form 1099-DIV
The brokerage account statement
The prospectus

questions.correct_answer: The prospectus

misconceptions.A: Confuses marketing with the legal disclosure
misconceptions.B: Confuses a tax form with the fund's disclosure
misconceptions.C: Shows holdings and value, not goals and fees

questions.feedback: The prospectus is the official description of a fund.

questions.set_title: Mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: When two funds hold nearly the same investments, the lower-cost fund usually leaves more of the return for the investor.
questions.question: Two S&P 500 index funds track the same index. Fund A charges 0.03%; Fund B charges 0.50%. Which is generally the better choice?

choices.text: Fund B, because a higher fee means better management
Either, because fees never matter
Fund A, because the holdings are nearly identical and it costs less
Fund B, because it has a longer track record shown in ads

questions.correct_answer: Fund A, because the holdings are nearly identical and it costs less
questions.feedback: For funds that track the same index, lower cost usually wins.

questions.set_title: Mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Indexes differ in what they include. The S&P 500 covers about 500 large U.S. companies; total market indexes include thousands of large, medium, and small companies.
questions.question: A "total stock market" index fund holds thousands of U.S. companies, large and small. How does it differ from an S&P 500 fund?

choices.text: It holds only 5 large U.S. companies
It includes smaller companies too
It holds only bonds
It cannot lose value

questions.correct_answer: It includes smaller companies too
questions.feedback: Total market funds are broader than the S&P 500.

questions.set_title: Mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: International funds hold companies in other countries, which can add diversification.
questions.question: An international index fund mainly adds what to a U.S. stock portfolio?

choices.text: Only U.S. government bonds
A guarantee against loss
Cash that is kept in banks in foreign countries
Companies based outside the United States

questions.correct_answer: Companies based outside the United States
questions.feedback: International funds diversify across countries.

questions.set_title: Mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Some mutual funds have minimum initial investments. ETFs usually require only the price of one share (or less, with fractional shares).
questions.question: A fund's minimum initial investment is $3,000, but its ETF version can be bought for the price of one share, $95. Sam has $200. Which can he buy?

choices.text: The mutual fund version
Both, because minimums do not apply to teens
The ETF version
Neither

questions.correct_answer: The ETF version
questions.feedback: $200 covers one $95 ETF share but not the $3,000 minimum.

questions.set_title: Mutual funds, ETFs, and index funds
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.question: Which question is MOST important when choosing a fund for a long-term goal?

choices.text: What does it hold, and what does it cost each year?
Did it have the best return of any fund last month?
Is it the most popular fund this month?
Do my friends own it?

questions.correct_answer: What does it hold, and what does it cost each year?
questions.feedback: Holdings and costs matter most for long-term results.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Explain diversification and asset allocation and compute a portfolio's weighted return
questions.intro: Diversification means spreading money across many investments so that a problem with one has a smaller effect on the whole. It can be across companies, industries, countries, and types of assets (stocks, bonds, cash). Diversification lowers risk but cannot eliminate it or guarantee against loss.
questions.question: Which portfolio is MOST diversified?

choices.text: Shares of one technology company
Three stocks, all airlines
A total market index fund plus a bond index fund
Shares of a single restaurant chain and its supplier

questions.correct_answer: A total market index fund plus a bond index fund
questions.feedback: Thousands of stocks plus bonds spread risk widely.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Explain diversification and asset allocation and compute a portfolio's weighted return
questions.intro: Asset allocation is how a portfolio is divided among asset classes such as stocks, bonds, and cash. A portfolio's return is the weighted average: (weight × return) for each part, added together.
questions.question: Jen's portfolio is 60% stocks and 40% bonds. Stocks return 8% and bonds 3% this year. What is the portfolio's return?

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Explain diversification and asset allocation and compute a portfolio's weighted return
questions.question: Which statement about diversification is TRUE?

choices.text: A diversified portfolio cannot lose value
It reduces the impact of any single investment but cannot prevent all losses
Diversification guarantees a profit every year
Owning more shares of one stock is diversification

questions.correct_answer: It reduces the impact of any single investment but cannot prevent all losses

misconceptions.A: Assumes a diversified investment cannot lose value

questions.feedback: Broad market declines can still lower a diversified portfolio.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Explain diversification and asset allocation and compute a portfolio's weighted return
questions.question: Jen has $10,000 invested: 60% stocks, 40% bonds. How much is in stocks?

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Explain diversification and asset allocation and compute a portfolio's weighted return
questions.intro: A longer time horizon allows more time to recover from stock market declines, so younger investors often hold more stocks. People nearing their goal often shift toward bonds and cash.
questions.question: Generally, which allocation fits a 20-year-old saving for retirement better than a 70-year-old retiree?

choices.text: More stocks, because the time horizon is longer
All cash, because young people cannot handle risk
All bonds, because stocks are illegal for young investors
Exactly the same allocation for everyone

questions.correct_answer: More stocks, because the time horizon is longer
questions.feedback: Longer horizons can usually tolerate more stock market risk.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: When all your money depends on one thing, a problem with that thing affects everything. Spreading out reduces the damage.
questions.question: A fruit stand sells only bananas. During a banana shortage it cannot get any bananas, so it cannot make sales. What happens?

choices.text: It is unaffected
It earns more because bananas are now scarce
Its insurance replaces the lost sales
Its whole business suffers

questions.correct_answer: Its whole business suffers

misconceptions.B: Ignores that it has no bananas to sell

questions.feedback: With only one product and none to sell, the whole business is hit.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Spreading sales across several products means a problem with one product affects only part of the business.
questions.question: A second stand sells bananas, apples, and oranges. During a banana shortage it cannot get bananas, but it can still get and sell apples and oranges. What happens?

choices.text: Only part of its business suffers
Its whole business suffers just as much
It earns nothing at all
It earns more on every fruit

questions.correct_answer: Only part of its business suffers

misconceptions.D: Assumes the shortage helps all products

questions.feedback: Selling several fruits spreads the risk.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.question: Which saying describes diversification?

choices.text: "Buy low, sell high."
"Slow and steady wins the race."
"A penny saved is a penny earned, my friend."
"Don't put all your eggs in one basket."

questions.correct_answer: "Don't put all your eggs in one basket."

misconceptions.A: A timing saying, not about spreading risk

questions.feedback: Spreading eggs across baskets limits the damage if one falls.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Diversification can happen across companies, industries, countries, and asset classes (broad types of investments, such as stocks, bonds, and cash).
questions.question: Jen owns stocks of 20 U.S. companies and adds a bond fund. What kind of diversification does the bond fund add?

choices.text: Across brokerage firms
Across asset classes
Across account types
Across more companies only

questions.correct_answer: Across asset classes

misconceptions.A: Confuses where you invest with what you own
misconceptions.D: Bonds are a different asset class, not just more companies

questions.feedback: Stocks and bonds are different asset classes.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Percent of an amount = amount × rate as a decimal.
questions.question: What is 40% of $5,000?

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Over time, investments grow at different rates, so a portfolio drifts away from its target allocation. Rebalancing means buying or selling to return to the target.
questions.question: Jen's target is 60% stocks, 40% bonds on $10,000. After a strong year, she has $7,200 in stocks and $3,800 in bonds. What percent is in stocks now (nearest whole percent)?

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Target amount = total value × target percent.
questions.question: To rebalance $11,000 to 60% stocks, what should the stock amount be?

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Amount to move = current amount − target amount.
questions.question: Jen's portfolio holds $7,200 in stocks, and her target for stocks is $6,600. How much stock should she sell (moving it to bonds)?

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Without rebalancing, a portfolio can become riskier than intended as stocks grow.
questions.question: Why rebalance?

choices.text: To guarantee higher returns
Because federal law requires it to be done each month
To keep risk at the level the investor chose
To avoid ever owning bonds

questions.correct_answer: To keep risk at the level the investor chose
questions.feedback: Rebalancing restores the chosen risk level.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Selling investments at a gain in a taxable account can create capital gains taxes.
questions.question: Instead of selling, Jen could rebalance by directing new contributions to bonds. Why might that be helpful in a taxable account?

choices.text: It can avoid selling and creating taxable gains
It earns guaranteed returns
It is required by the IRS
It removes all risk

questions.correct_answer: It can avoid selling and creating taxable gains
questions.feedback: Using new money to rebalance can avoid realizing gains.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Diversification works best when investments do not all move together. Assets that move the same way give little protection; assets that move differently reduce overall swings.
questions.question: Two stocks always rise and fall together. Does owning both diversify much?

choices.text: Yes, because there are now two different funds
Yes, completely
No, it doubles the risk
Not much, because they move the same way

questions.correct_answer: Not much, because they move the same way
questions.feedback: Investments that move together provide little diversification.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: High-quality bonds often behave differently from stocks, especially in downturns, though not always.
questions.question: Which pair is more likely to diversify a stock-heavy portfolio?

choices.text: Two technology stocks
Two airline stocks
Stocks and high-quality bonds
Two stock funds holding the same companies

questions.correct_answer: Stocks and high-quality bonds
questions.feedback: High-quality bonds often move differently from stocks.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Funds that track the same index hold the same companies, so owning several adds little diversification.
questions.question: Sam owns three different S&P 500 index funds. Is he well diversified across funds?

choices.text: Yes, owning three funds triples her overall diversification
Not really; the three funds hold almost the same stocks
Yes, because each has a different name
No, because index funds hold one stock

questions.correct_answer: Not really; the three funds hold almost the same stocks
questions.feedback: Overlapping funds add little real diversification.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Market risk affects nearly all stocks at once; diversification mainly reduces the risk of individual companies or industries.
questions.question: In a severe market crash, many stocks fall together. What does this show about diversification across stocks?

choices.text: Diversification always prevents losses
Diversified portfolios are immune to crashes
Bonds always fall more than stocks
It cannot remove market-wide risk

questions.correct_answer: It cannot remove market-wide risk
questions.feedback: Market-wide declines affect even diversified stock portfolios.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Target-date funds hold a mix of stock and bond funds and become more conservative over time.
questions.question: A target-date fund automatically shifts from stocks toward bonds as the target year approaches. What problem does it solve?

choices.text: It guarantees no losses before the target year
It removes all fees
It manages allocation and rebalancing for you
It invests only in cash

questions.correct_answer: It manages allocation and rebalancing for you
questions.feedback: Target-date funds automate allocation changes over time.

questions.set_title: Placing an order: market and limit orders
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Place basic investment orders and explain market orders, limit orders, and the bid-ask spread
questions.intro: To buy an investment, you place an order with your broker. A market order asks to buy or sell right away at the best available price. It usually executes quickly, but the exact price is not guaranteed and can differ from the last price you saw, especially in fast markets.
questions.question: Kai places a MARKET order to buy 10 shares. What does this mean?

choices.text: Buy only if the price falls to a set amount
Buy promptly at the best price available, which is not guaranteed
Buy at yesterday's closing price, guaranteed
Buy only after the market closes for the day

questions.correct_answer: Buy promptly at the best price available, which is not guaranteed
questions.feedback: Market orders prioritize speed, not a guaranteed price.

questions.set_title: Placing an order: market and limit orders
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Place basic investment orders and explain market orders, limit orders, and the bid-ask spread
questions.intro: A limit order sets the most you will pay (to buy) or the least you will accept (to sell). It executes only at the limit price or better, so it may not execute at all.
questions.question: Lia places a LIMIT order to buy at $50. The stock is trading at $52. What happens?

choices.text: The order fills only if the price falls to $50 or lower
It buys immediately at $52
It buys at $52 and refunds $2
It buys at exactly $50 no matter what the market price is

questions.correct_answer: The order fills only if the price falls to $50 or lower

misconceptions.D: Thinks the limit forces a price

questions.feedback: A buy limit at $50 fills only at $50 or less.

questions.set_title: Placing an order: market and limit orders
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Place basic investment orders and explain market orders, limit orders, and the bid-ask spread
questions.intro: The bid is the highest price buyers are offering; the ask is the lowest price sellers will accept. Buyers usually pay the ask, and sellers receive the bid. The difference is the bid-ask spread.
questions.question: A stock shows: bid $49.95, ask $50.05. If Omar places a market order to BUY, about what price will he pay?
questions.feedback: A market buy order typically fills near the ask, $50.05.

questions.set_title: Placing an order: market and limit orders
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Place basic investment orders and explain market orders, limit orders, and the bid-ask spread
questions.intro: The bid-ask spread = ask − bid. Narrow spreads mean lower trading costs.
questions.question: Using the bid of $49.95 and ask of $50.05, what is the bid-ask spread?

questions.set_title: Placing an order: market and limit orders
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Place basic investment orders and explain market orders, limit orders, and the bid-ask spread

questions.intro: Present bias is the tendency to value what is close in time over what is far away, which makes distant goals like retirement easy to postpone. Automatic payroll contributions help overcome it.

Present bias
Diversification
Inflation

questions.feedback: Putting off a distant goal in favor of current wants is present bias.

Waiting for a bonus

questions.intro: A 401(k) is a retirement plan offered by many private employers. A 403(b) is a similar plan offered by public schools, colleges, hospitals, and many nonprofits. Both let workers save part of each paycheck, often with tax benefits and sometimes an employer match.

Public schools and many nonprofit organizations

questions.unit_title: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s

questions.unit_title: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s

questions.unit_title: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.section_skill: Explain employer retirement plans, employer matching, and the cost of cashing out
questions.intro: When leaving a job, you can usually leave the money in the old plan, roll it into a new employer's plan, or roll it into an IRA. Cashing out before 59½ usually means income tax plus a 10% additional tax, unless an exception applies.
questions.question: Maya leaves a job with $10,000 in her 401(k) and is under 59½. If she cashes it out, assume 22% federal income tax plus a 10% additional tax for early withdrawal. How much is left?

questions.unit_title: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.section_skill: Explain employer retirement plans, employer matching, and the cost of cashing out

Cashing out and spending it
Withdrawing it to pay for a vacation
Having a check mailed and keeping it for a year

questions.feedback: A direct rollover of pre-tax money to a traditional IRA or pre-tax plan keeps taxes deferred, with no penalty.

questions.intro: When you leave a job, you can roll a 401(k) into an IRA or a new employer plan. Rolling pre-tax money into a Roth IRA is a conversion and is generally taxable.

misconceptions.D: Misses mandatory withholding on indirect rollovers

questions.unit_title: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s

questions.unit_title: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.intro: In an indirect rollover, the plan withholds 20%. To complete the rollover tax-free, the full original amount must be deposited within 60 days, making up the withheld part from other money.
questions.question: A worker's old plan pays out a $10,000 pre-tax distribution by check and withholds 20% ($2,000), so she receives $8,000. To avoid tax on any of the $10,000, how much must she deposit into an IRA within 60 days?

questions.intro: An IRA (individual retirement account, officially "arrangement") is a tax-advantaged retirement account. Traditional and Roth IRAs are usually opened by individuals themselves; some employers offer IRA-based plans such as SEP and SIMPLE IRAs. IRAs give tax advantages in exchange for rules about contributions and withdrawals, and the money can be invested in stocks, bonds, funds, and more.

choices.text: An insured checking account for retirees
A government pension that is paid to every American worker
An individual retirement account with tax advantages
A loan program for people near retirement

questions.unit_title: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s

questions.intro: Roth IRA withdrawals come out in a set order: regular contributions first, then conversion and rollover amounts (which have their own rules), then earnings. Nothing; the $5,000 comes from contributions
$3,000 of earnings
Only the 10% additional tax, which would be $500

misconceptions.A: Thinks every early withdrawal is taxed

questions.feedback: Her first $8,000 withdrawn counts as regular contributions, so $5,000 is tax- and penalty-free.

Any withdrawal at all, because Roth means tax-free

questions.intro: To see whether a tax is regressive, compare the tax paid with each person's income.
questions.question: Two people each buy $500 of taxable goods with a 6% sales tax. One earns $25,000 a year; the other earns $250,000. What percent of income does each pay in this tax?

misconceptions.A: Uses the tax rate instead of share of income
misconceptions.B: Assumes the tax depends on income

questions.feedback: Tax: $500 × 0.06 = $30 each. $30 ÷ $25,000 = 0.12%; $30 ÷ $250,000 = 0.012%. The lower earner pays a larger share, so this is regressive.

questions.intro: Applications usually require photo ID, proof of income (pay stubs or an offer letter), past landlord references, and consent to a credit and background check. An application fee is common.
questions.question: Which documents does a rental application commonly ask for?

choices.text: A high school diploma and report cards
ID, proof of income, rental history, and credit consent
A car title and insurance card
A list of friends' phone numbers

questions.correct_answer: ID, proof of income, rental history, and credit consent
questions.feedback: Landlords verify identity, income, history, and credit.

questions.section_skill: Estimate affordable rent and prepare a rental application
questions.intro: A guarantor agrees to pay the rent if the tenant does not. Deposit limits depend on state law.
questions.question: Mo has no rental history and a thin credit file. What might a landlord ask for?

choices.text: Nothing; landlords cannot ask for anything else
Proof that he has never borrowed money
His Social Security card mailed in
A guarantor (cosigner) or a larger deposit, where legal

questions.correct_answer: A guarantor (cosigner) or a larger deposit, where legal
questions.feedback: Guarantors (or deposits within legal limits) reduce the landlord's risk.

questions.intro: Percent of an amount = amount × rate as a decimal.
questions.question: What is 30% of $2,500?

questions.intro: Percent of income = rent ÷ income × 100.
questions.question: $900 rent on $3,000 monthly income is what percent?
Monthly income is $2,800. What is yearly income?

questions.intro: Under a "40 times rent" rule, the most rent = yearly income ÷ 40.
questions.question: Yearly income is $33,600. Dividing by 40 gives what monthly rent limit?

questions.intro: The 30% rent rule of thumb is a quick budgeting check. The government's formal "cost-burdened" measure counts total housing costs, including utilities, above 30% of income.
questions.question: A common rule of thumb flags spending more than 30% of income on rent. Why does that matter?

choices.text: Less money remains for other needs and saving
Landlords charge more to such tenants
It lowers credit scores automatically each month
It is illegal to rent above 30%

questions.correct_answer: Less money remains for other needs and saving
questions.feedback: High housing costs crowd out other needs and saving.

questions.intro: Move-in costs often include first month's rent, a security deposit, fees, and moving expenses, all due before or at move-in.
questions.question: Move-in costs: first month's rent $1,000, security deposit $1,500, and a $50 application fee. How much cash does Mo need?

questions.intro: Months needed = amount needed ÷ monthly saving, rounded up to a whole month.
questions.question: Mo saves $300 a month toward $2,550 of move-in costs. How many months until he has enough (rounded up)?

choices.text: 9 months
8 months
85 months
3 months

questions.correct_answer: 9 months

questions.intro: First apartments often need furniture, kitchen basics, and utility deposits or setup fees.
questions.question: Which expense is often forgotten in a first apartment budget?

choices.text: Rent
The lease itself
Rent for the first month, which the landlord already listed
Furniture, kitchen supplies, and utility setup fees

questions.correct_answer: Furniture, kitchen supplies, and utility setup fees
questions.feedback: One-time setup costs can be large.

questions.intro: Housing share = total housing costs ÷ income × 100.
questions.question: Mo's take-home pay is $2,500. Rent is $900, utilities $120, renters insurance $15, and internet $50. What share of take-home pay do these housing costs use (nearest whole percent)?
Which choice would most lower Mo's housing share?

choices.text: Adding cable TV
Finding a roommate to split rent and utilities
Taking a bigger unit so a future roommate can join later
Paying rent with a credit card

questions.correct_answer: Finding a roommate to split rent and utilities
questions.feedback: Splitting fixed costs is one of the biggest savings available.

questions.intro: Landlords may check credit reports (with permission). Some checks are recorded as inquiries.
questions.question: A landlord runs a credit check on Mo. Does this affect his credit score?

choices.text: It erases his credit history
It always drops his score by 100 points
It may appear as an inquiry; it does not reveal income
It shows his bank balances and pay to the landlord directly

questions.correct_answer: It may appear as an inquiry; it does not reveal income
questions.feedback: Tenant screening may add an inquiry; reports do not show income or bank balances.

questions.intro: The Fair Housing Act prohibits housing discrimination based on race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status, and disability. Some exemptions exist, such as certain senior housing.
questions.question: A landlord refuses to rent to a family because they have young children. Under the federal Fair Housing Act, this is…

choices.text: legal in every building
illegal discrimination based on familial status
allowed whenever the landlord prefers a quiet building
required by fire codes

questions.correct_answer: illegal discrimination based on familial status
questions.feedback: Familial status is a protected class under the Fair Housing Act.

questions.intro: HUD and state agencies enforce fair housing laws.
questions.question: Where can someone report housing discrimination?

choices.text: The IRS
The credit bureau that reported his score
HUD or the state civil rights agency
The landlord's friend

questions.correct_answer: HUD or the state civil rights agency
questions.feedback: HUD and state agencies accept fair housing complaints.

questions.intro: When a landlord takes adverse action based on a consumer report, the applicant must be told and can get a free copy of the report.
questions.question: A landlord denies Mo because of information in a tenant screening report. What right does Mo have under federal law?

choices.text: None at all
To have the landlord approve him anyway
To sue the landlord for checking
To be told and to get a free copy to dispute errors

questions.correct_answer: To be told and to get a free copy to dispute errors
questions.feedback: Adverse action notices let applicants check and dispute reports.

questions.intro: Under a "monthly income at least 3× rent" rule, the most rent = monthly income ÷ 3.
questions.question: Mo earns $2,800 a month. A landlord requires monthly income of 3 times the rent. What is the highest rent he qualifies for?

questions.set_title: Reading a lease and security deposits
questions.section_skill: Read key lease terms and apply security deposit rules
questions.intro: A lease lists the rent, due date, grace period, late fees, length of the lease, who pays which utilities, rules (pets, guests, noise), maintenance duties, renewal terms, and what happens if you leave early. Read every section before signing.
questions.question: A lease says: "Rent $1,100 due on the 1st. Late fee $50 if not received by the 5th." Jen pays on the 7th. What does she owe for that month?

questions.set_title: Reading a lease and security deposits
questions.section_skill: Read key lease terms and apply security deposit rules
questions.intro: A security deposit protects the landlord against unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear and tear. It is generally returned, minus allowed deductions, after the lease ends. State laws limit amounts and set return deadlines.
questions.question: A security deposit is…

choices.text: money held to cover unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear
a fee the landlord keeps no matter what condition the unit is in
the last month's rent, automatically
a payment for the landlord's insurance

questions.correct_answer: money held to cover unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear
questions.feedback: Deposits are held and returned minus allowed deductions.

questions.set_title: Reading a lease and security deposits
questions.section_skill: Read key lease terms and apply security deposit rules
questions.intro: New Jersey law caps security deposits at 1.5 months' rent. Other states have different limits.
questions.question: In New Jersey, a security deposit may not exceed 1.5 times one month's rent. Rent is $1,200. What is the largest deposit allowed?

questions.set_title: Reading a lease and security deposits
questions.section_skill: Read key lease terms and apply security deposit rules
questions.intro: Normal wear and tear (small nail holes, faded paint) is generally not deducted. Damage beyond that can be. New Jersey requires the landlord to return the deposit with interest, less itemized charges, within 30 days after the lease ends.
questions.question: Jen's lease ends. Her $1,500 deposit has $200 deducted for a broken door and $0 for small nail holes. In New Jersey, about how much should she get back, and by when?

choices.text: $1,500 within one year
$0, because deposits are never returned
$1,300 (plus any interest) within 30 days
$1,300 whenever the landlord chooses to pay

questions.correct_answer: $1,300 (plus any interest) within 30 days

misconceptions.A: Ignores the deduction and the deadline

questions.feedback: $1,500 − $200 = $1,300, plus any interest, with an itemized list, within 30 days in New Jersey.

questions.set_title: Reading a lease and security deposits
questions.section_skill: Read key lease terms and apply security deposit rules
questions.question: Which lease term should Jen check before getting a pet?

choices.text: The renters insurance deductible only
The pet policy and any pet deposit or monthly pet fee
Only the monthly rent, since pets never change lease terms
The parking rules for guests

questions.correct_answer: The pet policy and any pet deposit or monthly pet fee
questions.feedback: Pet rules and fees are set in the lease.

questions.set_title: Reading a lease and security deposits
questions.intro: The lease term is the length of the agreement.
questions.question: A lease runs from August 1 to July 31. How long is it?

choices.text: 6 months
11 months
24 months
12 months

questions.correct_answer: 12 months
questions.feedback: August 1 to July 31 is 12 months.

questions.set_title: Reading a lease and security deposits
questions.intro: Leases assign each bill to the landlord or tenant.
questions.question: "Tenant pays electricity and gas; landlord pays water." Who pays the water bill?

choices.text: The landlord
The tenant who lives there
The city
Neither

questions.correct_answer: The landlord
questions.feedback: The lease assigns water to the landlord.

questions.set_title: Reading a lease and security deposits
questions.intro: A grace period is a short time after a due date during which payment is still accepted without a late fee.
questions.question: A "grace period" for rent means…

choices.text: days after the due date before a late fee applies
a discount for paying early
a free month of rent
a period at the start of the lease when rent is not owed

questions.correct_answer: days after the due date before a late fee applies
questions.feedback: Grace periods delay late fees for a few days.

questions.set_title: Reading a lease and security deposits
questions.question: 1.5 times $1,000 is…

questions.set_title: Reading a lease and security deposits
questions.question: Why should Jen read a lease BEFORE signing?

choices.text: Leases can be changed by the tenant alone later
Signing makes her legally bound to its terms
Only the landlord is bound by a lease
Leases are not legal documents

questions.correct_answer: Signing makes her legally bound to its terms

misconceptions.A: Believes one party can change a contract

questions.feedback: A signed lease is a binding contract.

questions.set_title: Reading a lease and security deposits
questions.intro: A move-in checklist and dated photos protect your deposit by recording existing damage.
questions.question: Why should Jen document the unit's condition with dated photos at move-in?

choices.text: To post them online for future renters
To ask the landlord to lower the rent right away
Because photos replace the need for a lease
To show which damage existed before she moved in

questions.correct_answer: To show which damage existed before she moved in
questions.feedback: Records prove pre-existing damage so it is not charged to you.

questions.set_title: Reading a lease and security deposits
questions.intro: Deductions generally cover damage beyond normal wear and tear, plus unpaid rent.
questions.question: Which charge is MOST likely to be allowed from a deposit?

choices.text: Small nail holes from hanging pictures
Faded paint after three years
Replacing a carpet ruined by a pet
Minor scuffs on floors

questions.correct_answer: Replacing a carpet ruined by a pet
questions.feedback: Pet damage is beyond normal wear and tear.

questions.set_title: Reading a lease and security deposits
questions.intro: Landlords need a forwarding address to return deposits and statements.
questions.question: At move-out, Jen cleans, returns keys, and gives a forwarding address. Why the address?

choices.text: So the landlord can mail her future bills
So the landlord can send the deposit and itemized list
Because a forwarding address raises the deposit refund
To end her renters insurance

questions.correct_answer: So the landlord can send the deposit and itemized list
questions.feedback: A forwarding address ensures the deposit reaches her.

questions.set_title: Reading a lease and security deposits
questions.intro: New Jersey requires deposits to be held in an interest-bearing account, with interest credited to the tenant.
questions.question: Jen's deposit of $1,800 earned 1% interest for one year in New Jersey. About how much interest is owed?

questions.set_title: Reading a lease and security deposits
questions.intro: Tenants can pursue unreturned deposits; New Jersey law provides remedies when deposits are wrongfully withheld.
questions.question: A landlord keeps a deposit without explanation past the legal deadline. What can a New Jersey tenant do?

choices.text: Nothing
Post a bad review and wait
Take the landlord's property
Request it in writing, then use small claims court if needed

questions.correct_answer: Request it in writing, then use small claims court if needed
questions.feedback: Written requests and small claims court are common remedies.

questions.set_title: Reading a lease and security deposits
questions.section_skill: Breaking a lease, renewals, and roommates
questions.intro: Leaving early can mean paying rent until a new tenant is found or paying an early-termination fee, depending on the lease and state law.
questions.question: Jen must move 4 months before her 12-month lease ends. Rent is $1,100. If the lease makes her liable for remaining rent until the unit is re-rented, and it takes 2 months to re-rent, how much might she owe?

questions.set_title: Reading a lease and security deposits
questions.section_skill: Breaking a lease, renewals, and roommates
questions.intro: Leases often require advance written notice to end or renew.
questions.question: Jen's lease renews automatically unless she gives 60 days' written notice. Her lease ends June 30. By about when must she give notice to leave?

choices.text: Early May
June 29
July 15
There is no deadline

questions.correct_answer: Early May
questions.feedback: 60 days before June 30 is about May 1.

questions.set_title: Reading a lease and security deposits
questions.section_skill: Breaking a lease, renewals, and roommates
questions.intro: When roommates sign the same lease, each is often responsible for the full rent ("joint and several" liability).
questions.question: Two roommates sign one lease for $1,600 rent. One stops paying. What can the landlord usually do?

choices.text: Collect only half from each roommate, no matter what
Collect from the paying roommate only her half
Hold either roommate responsible for the full rent
Lower the rent to $800

questions.correct_answer: Hold either roommate responsible for the full rent
questions.feedback: On a joint lease, each tenant can be held responsible for all of the rent.

questions.set_title: Reading a lease and security deposits
questions.section_skill: Breaking a lease, renewals, and roommates
questions.intro: Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100.
questions.question: A landlord offers a renewal with rent rising from $1,100 to $1,155. What is the percent increase?

questions.set_title: Reading a lease and security deposits
questions.section_skill: Breaking a lease, renewals, and roommates
questions.intro: Many leases require the landlord's written permission to sublet.
questions.question: Subletting means…

choices.text: the landlord selling the building
paying rent late
renting your unit to someone else while still the tenant
breaking the lease with no notice

questions.correct_answer: renting your unit to someone else while still the tenant
questions.feedback: Subletting puts another person in your unit under your lease; check the lease first.

questions.set_title: Tenant responsibilities, rights, and renters insurance
questions.section_skill: Explain tenant duties and rights and evaluate renters insurance
questions.intro: A landlord's insurance covers the building, not tenants' belongings. Renters insurance covers your personal property (for theft, fire, and other listed causes) and liability if someone is injured in your home or you damage others' property. It often costs about $10–$25 a month.
questions.question: Jen's belongings are stolen from her apartment. The landlord has building insurance. Which policy covers HER belongings?

choices.text: Her own renters insurance policy
The landlord's building insurance
The city's emergency fund
Her car insurance, for anything inside a home

questions.correct_answer: Her own renters insurance policy

misconceptions.B: Covers the building, not tenant property

questions.feedback: Tenant belongings are covered only by the tenant's renters insurance.

questions.set_title: Tenant responsibilities, rights, and renters insurance
questions.section_skill: Explain tenant duties and rights and evaluate renters insurance
questions.intro: A premium is what you pay for the policy. A deductible is the amount you pay toward a claim before insurance pays the rest.
questions.question: Jen's renters policy costs $16 a month with a $500 deductible. A fire destroys $4,000 of her belongings (covered). How much does the insurer pay?

questions.set_title: Tenant responsibilities, rights, and renters insurance
questions.section_skill: Explain tenant duties and rights and evaluate renters insurance
questions.intro: Tenants generally must pay rent on time, keep the unit clean, avoid damage, follow the lease, and report repairs. Landlords generally must keep the unit safe and livable (heat, water, structural repairs) and follow notice rules.
questions.question: Which is usually the TENANT's responsibility?

choices.text: Replacing the building's roof
Fixing a broken furnace or a leaking water heater herself
Paying the building's property tax
Keeping the unit clean and reporting problems promptly

questions.correct_answer: Keeping the unit clean and reporting problems promptly
questions.feedback: Tenants keep the unit clean and report problems.

questions.set_title: Tenant responsibilities, rights, and renters insurance
questions.section_skill: Explain tenant duties and rights and evaluate renters insurance
questions.intro: Landlords must keep homes habitable, including heat. Tenants should report problems in writing and keep records. State law sets remedies if repairs are not made.
questions.question: In winter, Jen's heat stops working. What should she do FIRST?

choices.text: Stop paying rent immediately
Notify the landlord in writing and keep a copy
Hire a contractor and deduct any cost she chooses
Wait until spring

questions.correct_answer: Notify the landlord in writing and keep a copy

misconceptions.A: Can violate the lease without proper steps

questions.feedback: A written notice creates a record and starts the repair process.

questions.set_title: Tenant responsibilities, rights, and renters insurance
questions.section_skill: Explain tenant duties and rights and evaluate renters insurance
questions.question: Over a year, how much does a $16-per-month renters policy cost?
questions.feedback: $16 × 12 = $192, often far less than replacing belongings.

questions.set_title: Tenant responsibilities, rights, and renters insurance
questions.intro: The premium is the price of insurance, paid monthly or yearly. The deductible is what you pay out of pocket on a claim before insurance pays.
questions.question: What is an insurance PREMIUM?

choices.text: The amount paid regularly to keep the policy
The amount the policyholder pays toward each claim first
The maximum the insurer pays
A refund from the insurer

questions.correct_answer: The amount paid regularly to keep the policy
questions.feedback: The premium is the regular cost of the policy.

questions.set_title: Tenant responsibilities, rights, and renters insurance
questions.question: What is a DEDUCTIBLE?

choices.text: The monthly cost of the policy
The most the insurer will pay
The amount you pay on a claim before insurance pays
A bonus the insurer pays you when you file no claims

questions.correct_answer: The amount you pay on a claim before insurance pays
questions.feedback: The deductible comes out of your pocket on each claim.

questions.set_title: Tenant responsibilities, rights, and renters insurance
questions.intro: Insurance pays the loss minus the deductible.
questions.question: A covered $1,200 loss with a $250 deductible is paid how?

choices.text: Insurance pays $1,200
You pay $250; insurance pays $950
You pay $950; insurance pays $250
You pay $1,200

questions.correct_answer: You pay $250; insurance pays $950
questions.feedback: $1,200 − $250 = $950 paid by insurance.

questions.set_title: Tenant responsibilities, rights, and renters insurance
questions.intro: Taking on more cost per claim (higher deductible) usually lowers the premium.
questions.question: Which choice usually LOWERS the premium?

choices.text: Choosing a much lower deductible
Adding more coverage
Filing more claims
Choosing a higher deductible

questions.correct_answer: Choosing a higher deductible
questions.feedback: Higher deductible → lower premium.

questions.set_title: Tenant responsibilities, rights, and renters insurance
questions.question: Which loss is MOST likely covered by renters insurance?

choices.text: A laptop stolen in a break-in
Wear on old furniture over years
The building's cracked foundation
A planned vacation

questions.correct_answer: A laptop stolen in a break-in
questions.feedback: Theft of personal property is a typical covered loss.

questions.set_title: Tenant responsibilities, rights, and renters insurance
questions.intro: A home inventory, a list of belongings with values, helps choose coverage and file claims.
questions.question: Jen lists her belongings: electronics $2,500, furniture $1,800, clothes $1,500, other $1,200. How much personal property coverage does she need at minimum?

questions.set_title: Tenant responsibilities, rights, and renters insurance
questions.intro: Policies may pay replacement cost (new item) or actual cash value (replacement cost minus depreciation). Replacement cost policies usually cost more.
questions.question: "Replacement cost" coverage pays to replace items with new ones. "Actual cash value" pays…

choices.text: double the original price, to cover the cost of shopping
what the items were worth after depreciation
the item's original price
the price of a used item of any age

questions.correct_answer: what the items were worth after depreciation
questions.feedback: Actual cash value subtracts depreciation.

questions.set_title: Tenant responsibilities, rights, and renters insurance
questions.intro: Actual cash value = today's replacement cost − depreciation. Replacement cost coverage pays the full replacement cost instead.
questions.question: A 4-year-old TV would cost $1,000 to replace with a similar new one today. The policy figures its depreciation at 60%. Under actual cash value, before the deductible, what is it worth?

questions.set_title: Tenant responsibilities, rights, and renters insurance
questions.intro: Liability coverage helps pay if you are legally responsible for injuring someone or damaging their property.
questions.question: A guest slips in Jen's apartment and is hurt. Which part of renters insurance may help?

choices.text: Personal property coverage
Loss-of-use coverage
Nothing; insurance never covers injuries
Liability coverage

questions.correct_answer: Liability coverage
questions.feedback: Liability coverage addresses injuries to others.

questions.set_title: Tenant responsibilities, rights, and renters insurance
questions.intro: Loss-of-use coverage pays extra living costs when a covered event makes your home unlivable.
questions.question: After a covered fire, Jen must stay in a hotel for 2 weeks. Which coverage may help pay?

choices.text: Liability coverage for injuries to guests
The landlord's security deposit
Loss of use (additional living expenses)
Health insurance

questions.correct_answer: Loss of use (additional living expenses)
questions.feedback: Loss-of-use pays temporary living costs.

questions.set_title: Tenant responsibilities, rights, and renters insurance
questions.section_skill: Tenant rights and when to get help

No; self-help evictions are generally illegal
Yes, with one day's notice
Yes, if the lease allows it

questions.set_title: Tenant responsibilities, rights, and renters insurance
questions.section_skill: Tenant rights and when to get help

questions.question: A landlord wants to enter Jen's apartment for a non-emergency repair. What is generally expected?

A full month's written notice before every visit, even emergencies
Reasonable advance notice, as set by law or the lease
Permission from the city

questions.set_title: Tenant responsibilities, rights, and renters insurance

New Jersey's official "Truth in Renting" guide

questions.set_title: Tenant responsibilities, rights, and renters insurance
questions.section_skill: Tenant rights and when to get help

questions.question: Jen receives an eviction notice she believes is wrong. Which step is MOST important?

Ignore it
Move out immediately without responding to it
Stop paying rent

questions.set_title: Renting versus owning, and what a mortgage is

Insurance that protects a home and its contents from fire
A loan to buy a home, with the home as collateral
A savings account for a down payment

questions.feedback: A mortgage is a home loan secured by the home.

Payments can build equity (ownership) over time

It is easier to move on short notice when owning

choices.text: The home being bought
The buyer's car

The buyer's future salary

questions.set_title: Renting versus owning, and what a mortgage is
