questions.unit_title: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.section_skill: Explain lease terms and compare the cost of leasing with buying
questions.intro: Capitalized cost is the lease's agreed price. Residual value is the predicted value at the end. The payment covers the depreciation (cap cost − residual) spread over the months, plus a finance charge and tax.
questions.question: A car has a capitalized cost of $30,000 and a residual value of $18,000 after 36 months. What is the monthly depreciation part of the payment?

questions.unit_title: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.section_skill: Explain lease terms and compare the cost of leasing with buying
questions.intro: Total lease cost = amount due at signing + all monthly payments + any other charges. Check whether the amount due at signing already includes the first payment, so it is not counted twice.
questions.question: A lease needs $2,000 at signing, an upfront charge separate from the payments, plus 36 monthly payments of $399. Counting only these amounts, what is the total cost of the lease?

misconceptions.B: Leaves out the amount due at signing

questions.unit_title: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.section_skill: Explain lease terms and compare the cost of leasing with buying
questions.intro: Leasing tends to fit drivers who stay under mileage limits, keep the car in good shape, and like changing cars every few years. Buying fits drivers who keep cars a long time.
questions.question: Who is usually a better fit for leasing?

choices.text: A driver who goes 25,000 miles a year and keeps cars a decade
A buyer who wants to customize the car and own it outright
A person who wants never to have a monthly car payment
A low-mileage driver who wants a new car often

questions.correct_answer: A low-mileage driver who wants a new car often
questions.feedback: Leasing fits low mileage and frequent upgrades.

questions.unit_title: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.intro: The lease contract states a purchase option price, often equal to the residual value.
questions.question: At the end of a lease, what can the driver usually do?

choices.text: Return the car or buy it at the set price
Keep the car free of charge forever
Sell the car and keep the money
Stop paying and drive it until it finally breaks

questions.correct_answer: Return the car or buy it at the set price

misconceptions.C: The driver does not own it

questions.feedback: Return the car or buy it at the contract price.

questions.unit_title: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.question: In a lease, what is the residual value?

choices.text: The amount paid up front at signing
The predicted value at the end
The monthly finance charge
The car's price when new

questions.correct_answer: The predicted value at the end
questions.feedback: Residual value is the expected value when the lease ends.

questions.unit_title: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.intro: Lessees return the car in the condition the lease requires. Dents, stains, and worn tires beyond the standard can be charged.
questions.question: What are "excess wear and tear" charges?

choices.text: Monthly fees for routine oil changes
Taxes on the car's registration
Fees for damage beyond normal use
Charges for driving under the mileage limit

questions.correct_answer: Fees for damage beyond normal use
questions.feedback: Damage beyond normal wear is charged at return.

questions.unit_title: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.question: A lease costs $350 a month for 36 months. How much are the payments in total?

questions.unit_title: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.intro: Equity is the value you own. Loan payments build equity; lease payments do not.
questions.question: After paying off a car loan, the owner has the car. After a lease ends, what does the driver own?

choices.text: Half of the car's value
The car, with no further cost
Nothing, unless they buy the car
A credit toward any future purchase

questions.correct_answer: Nothing, unless they buy the car
questions.feedback: A lease builds no ownership; a paid-off loan does.

questions.unit_title: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.intro: Leases state the finance charge as a money factor, a small decimal. Money factor × 2,400 is roughly the equivalent APR.
questions.question: A lease has a money factor of 0.0025. Multiply by 2,400 to compare with an APR. What APR does it equal?

misconceptions.A: Reads the money factor as a percent

questions.unit_title: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.question: The monthly finance charge is (cap cost + residual) × money factor. For $30,000 and $18,000 with a money factor of 0.0025, what is it?

questions.unit_title: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.question: Depreciation is $333.33 a month and the finance charge is $120. What is the monthly payment before tax?

questions.unit_title: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.intro: If a leased car is totaled early, insurance and GAP coverage pay the leasing company; money paid up front is usually not returned.
questions.question: Why do some experts advise against a large down payment on a lease?

choices.text: Down payments on leases earn very high interest
It may be lost if the car is totaled
Leasing companies are not allowed to accept them
It always raises the monthly payment

questions.correct_answer: It may be lost if the car is totaled

misconceptions.A: Confuses a down payment with savings

questions.feedback: Cash paid up front on a lease can be lost if the car is totaled.

questions.unit_title: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.intro: Ending a lease early often triggers large fees, sometimes most of the remaining payments.
questions.question: Maya wants to end her lease after 18 of 36 months. What should she expect?

choices.text: Early termination charges
A refund of every payment made so far
No cost, since leases can end at any time
Ownership of half the car

questions.correct_answer: Early termination charges
questions.feedback: Early termination usually costs a lot; read that section before signing.

questions.unit_title: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.section_skill: Lease or buy: the three-year comparison
questions.intro: Equity = value − amount owed.
questions.question: After 3 years of buying, Maya's car is worth $18,000 and she still owes $6,000. What is her equity?

questions.unit_title: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.section_skill: Lease or buy: the three-year comparison
questions.intro: Net cost = total paid − equity kept, because the equity is value she still owns.
questions.question: Over 3 years, buying cost Maya $3,000 down plus 36 payments of $500. Her equity is $12,000. What is the net cost of buying for those 3 years?

questions.unit_title: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.section_skill: Lease or buy: the three-year comparison
questions.question: Leasing a car for 3 years costs $16,364 in total. Buying has a net cost of $9,000. Which costs less, and by how much?

choices.text: Leasing, by $7,364
Buying, by $25,364
Leasing, by $9,000
Buying, by $7,364

questions.correct_answer: Buying, by $7,364

questions.unit_title: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.section_skill: Lease or buy: the three-year comparison
questions.intro: A lease payment covers the car's expected loss in value over the lease, a finance (rent) charge, and taxes and fees. A loan payment repays the full purchase price plus interest.
questions.question: Why are lease payments often lower than loan payments on the same car?

choices.text: Leasing companies do not charge any interest
Leased cars are exempt from every tax
You pay for expected depreciation plus a finance charge, not the full price
Leases last longer than loans

questions.correct_answer: You pay for expected depreciation plus a finance charge, not the full price
questions.feedback: A lease covers depreciation, a rent charge, and taxes and fees, not the whole price, so payments are often lower.

questions.unit_title: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.section_skill: Lease or buy: the three-year comparison
questions.subtopic: Matching the choice to the driver
questions.question: Maya drives 20,000 miles a year and keeps cars for 8 years. Which choice likely costs her less?

choices.text: Buying
Leasing, since mileage charges are always waived
Leasing a new car every year for eight years
Renting daily for eight years

questions.correct_answer: Buying
questions.feedback: High mileage and long ownership favor buying.

questions.set_title: Risk and the purpose of insurance
questions.section_skill: Identify risk management strategies and explain how insurance transfers financial risk
questions.intro: Four ways to manage risk: avoid it (do not do the risky thing), reduce it (make a loss less likely or smaller), retain it (pay for losses yourself), or transfer it (pay someone else, usually an insurer, to take the loss). Insurance is risk transfer.
questions.question: Luis pays a company $40 a month so that if his phone is stolen, the company pays for a replacement. Which risk strategy is this?

choices.text: Avoiding the risk by never owning a phone at all
Transferring the risk
Reducing the risk by using a stronger case
Keeping the risk and paying for losses himself

questions.correct_answer: Transferring the risk

misconceptions.A: Avoiding means not doing the risky thing
misconceptions.C: Reducing lowers the chance or size of a loss

questions.feedback: Insurance moves the cost of a loss to the insurer in exchange for a premium.

questions.set_title: Risk and the purpose of insurance
questions.section_skill: Identify risk management strategies and explain how insurance transfers financial risk
questions.intro: Key terms: the premium is what you pay for coverage (monthly or yearly). A claim is your request for payment after a loss. The deductible is the part of a covered loss you pay before the insurer pays.
questions.question: In insurance, what does the word "premium" mean?

choices.text: The money the insurer pays after a covered loss
The part of a loss the policyholder pays first
A bonus paid to drivers with no accidents
The price paid for coverage

questions.correct_answer: The price paid for coverage

misconceptions.A: Confuses premium with a claim payment

questions.feedback: The premium is the cost of the policy.

questions.set_title: Risk and the purpose of insurance
questions.section_skill: Identify risk management strategies and explain how insurance transfers financial risk
questions.intro: For most property losses, the policyholder pays the deductible and the insurer pays the rest, up to the policy limit.
questions.question: A covered loss costs $3,000. Luis's deductible is $500. How much does the insurer pay?

questions.set_title: Risk and the purpose of insurance
questions.section_skill: Identify risk management strategies and explain how insurance transfers financial risk
questions.intro: Insurance pools risk: many people each pay a small, predictable premium, and the pool pays the few who have large losses.
questions.question: How can insurers afford to pay large losses?

choices.text: The government refunds every claim the insurer pays
Insurers only sell to people who never have losses
Many people's premiums pool together
Policyholders repay the claim later with interest

questions.correct_answer: Many people's premiums pool together
questions.feedback: Pooling many premiums covers the few large losses.

questions.set_title: Risk and the purpose of insurance
questions.section_skill: Identify risk management strategies and explain how insurance transfers financial risk
questions.intro: Insurance matters most for losses that are unlikely but too large to afford. Small, affordable losses are often cheaper to retain, especially with an emergency fund.
questions.question: Which loss is most sensible to retain (pay yourself) rather than insure?

choices.text: A house fire that destroys everything you own
A crash that injures another driver badly
A long illness with large hospital bills
A $15 phone charger that breaks

questions.correct_answer: A $15 phone charger that breaks
questions.feedback: Retain small losses; insure the ones that could be financially devastating.

questions.set_title: Risk and the purpose of insurance
questions.question: Which word describes a chance of losing money or something of value?

choices.text: Equity
Risk
Liquidity
Principal

questions.correct_answer: Risk
questions.feedback: Risk is the chance of loss.

questions.set_title: Risk and the purpose of insurance
questions.intro: Reducing risk makes a loss less likely or less severe, such as seat belts, smoke alarms, or locks.
questions.question: Wearing a seat belt is which risk strategy?

choices.text: Reducing the risk
Transferring the risk to another person
Avoiding the risk entirely
Retaining the risk on purpose

questions.correct_answer: Reducing the risk

misconceptions.B: No one else takes the loss
misconceptions.C: You still ride in the car
misconceptions.D: You are actively making the loss smaller

questions.feedback: Seat belts make injuries less severe: risk reduction.

questions.set_title: Risk and the purpose of insurance
questions.question: An event has a 1 in 50 chance of happening each year. What is that as a percent?

misconceptions.A: Leaves it as a decimal and adds a percent sign

questions.set_title: Risk and the purpose of insurance
questions.question: Which situation is risk avoidance?

choices.text: Buying a helmet before riding
Choosing not to ride a motorcycle
Buying motorcycle insurance before riding
Saving to pay for any damage

questions.correct_answer: Choosing not to ride a motorcycle
questions.feedback: Not doing the activity avoids its risk.

questions.set_title: Risk and the purpose of insurance
questions.question: Why does an emergency fund help with risk?

choices.text: It replaces the need for any insurance at all
It lowers the chance an accident happens
It covers small losses and deductibles
It earns enough to pay any lawsuit

questions.correct_answer: It covers small losses and deductibles

misconceptions.B: Money does not change the odds

questions.feedback: Cash on hand lets you retain small losses and pay deductibles.

questions.set_title: Risk and the purpose of insurance
questions.intro: A policy limit is the most an insurer will pay for a covered loss. The deductible is subtracted from the loss first; the insurer then pays the result, but never more than the limit.
questions.question: A renters policy has a $20,000 limit for personal property. A fire destroys $26,000 of belongings, and the deductible is $500. How much does the insurer pay?

misconceptions.D: Ignores the limit and the deductible
misconceptions.A: Subtracts the deductible from the limit

questions.set_title: Risk and the purpose of insurance
questions.intro: Exclusions list what a policy does not cover. Flood insurance, for example, is usually a separate policy.
questions.question: A policy lists "Exclusions: flood, earthquake." What does that mean?

choices.text: Those losses are not covered
Those losses are covered with no deductible
Those losses are covered only on weekends
Those losses are paid at double the limit

questions.correct_answer: Those losses are not covered
questions.feedback: Excluded losses are not covered.

questions.set_title: Risk and the purpose of insurance
questions.intro: The declarations ("dec") page shows who and what is covered, the limits, deductibles, and the premium.
questions.question: What is the declarations page of a policy?

choices.text: A letter saying a claim was denied
A form to cancel the policy
A list of every claim you have filed
A summary of coverage, limits, and premium

questions.correct_answer: A summary of coverage, limits, and premium
questions.feedback: The dec page summarizes the policy.

questions.set_title: Risk and the purpose of insurance
questions.intro: Replacement cost policies cost more but pay enough to replace items new.
questions.question: Replacement cost coverage pays to buy a new item; actual cash value pays the item's value minus depreciation. A 4-year-old TV cost $800 and is now worth $300. Under actual cash value, before any deductible, what is paid?
questions.feedback: Actual cash value pays the depreciated value, $300.

questions.set_title: Risk and the purpose of insurance
questions.intro: Contact the insurer promptly, take photos, keep receipts, and prevent further damage.
questions.question: After a covered loss, what is a sound first step in filing a claim?

choices.text: Throw away damaged items before anyone sees them
Wait a year to see if more damage appears
Document the damage with photos
Exaggerate the loss to cover the deductible

questions.correct_answer: Document the damage with photos
questions.feedback: Photos and receipts support a claim.

questions.section_skill: Calculate costs under a health plan and compare plans using premium, deductible, coinsurance, and out-of-pocket maximum
questions.intro: Health plans share costs based on the allowed (negotiated) in-network amount. You pay the deductible first. After that, coinsurance means you pay a percent and the plan pays the rest, until you reach the out-of-pocket maximum; then the plan pays 100% of covered in-network costs for the rest of the plan year.
questions.question: Ana's plan has a $1,500 deductible and 20% coinsurance after it, with a $5,000 out-of-pocket maximum. She has spent nothing yet this plan year. A hospital stay has an allowed in-network charge of $10,000 that follows these rules. How much does Ana pay?

questions.section_skill: Calculate costs under a health plan and compare plans using premium, deductible, coinsurance, and out-of-pocket maximum
questions.intro: The out-of-pocket maximum caps what you pay for covered in-network care in a plan year (premiums not included).
questions.question: Ana's plan: $1,500 deductible, 20% coinsurance, $5,000 out-of-pocket maximum. In a separate example, with no earlier spending this plan year, a covered in-network stay has an allowed charge of $40,000. How much does Ana pay?

misconceptions.C: Takes 20% of the bill and ignores the maximum

questions.feedback: $1,500 + 20% × $38,500 = $9,200, but the cap limits her share to $5,000.

questions.section_skill: Calculate costs under a health plan and compare plans using premium, deductible, coinsurance, and out-of-pocket maximum
questions.intro: A copay is a flat amount, such as $30 for a doctor visit or $10 for a generic prescription.
questions.question: What is a copay?

choices.text: A set dollar amount for a service
A percent of the bill paid after the deductible
The monthly price of the plan
The yearly limit on what you pay

questions.correct_answer: A set dollar amount for a service
questions.feedback: A copay is a fixed fee per service.

questions.section_skill: Calculate costs under a health plan and compare plans using premium, deductible, coinsurance, and out-of-pocket maximum
questions.intro: Under the Affordable Care Act, young adults can generally stay on a parent's plan until age 26, even if married, not living at home, or not a dependent for taxes.
questions.question: Ana is 22 and her parent has a family health plan. Under federal rules, until what age can she generally stay on it?
questions.feedback: Coverage on a parent's plan generally lasts until 26.

questions.section_skill: Calculate costs under a health plan and compare plans using premium, deductible, coinsurance, and out-of-pocket maximum
questions.intro: Insurers negotiate lower prices with in-network providers. Out-of-network care may cost much more or not be covered.
questions.question: Why does staying in network usually matter?

choices.text: Out-of-network doctors are not licensed to treat patients
In-network care costs the patient less
In-network care never needs any deductible
Network rules only matter for dental care

questions.correct_answer: In-network care costs the patient less
questions.feedback: Network providers have negotiated rates, so patients pay less.

questions.question: Which health plan cost is paid every month, even if you never see a doctor?

choices.text: The deductible, paid before coverage starts
Coinsurance, a percent of bills after the deductible
A copay, charged per visit
The premium

questions.correct_answer: The premium

misconceptions.A: Paid only when you get care

questions.feedback: Premiums are paid whether or not you use care.

questions.question: 20% of a $500 bill is…
Ana has paid $900 of her $1,500 deductible. How much more must she pay before coinsurance starts?

questions.intro: Once you reach the out-of-pocket maximum, the plan pays 100% of covered in-network costs for the rest of the plan year. Premiums are still owed.
questions.question: After Ana reaches her out-of-pocket maximum, what does she pay for covered in-network care that year?

choices.text: The full price of each visit
20% of each bill as before
The deductible again for each visit

questions.feedback: After the maximum, the plan pays 100% of covered costs.

questions.question: A plan has a high deductible but a low premium. Who might it suit?

choices.text: A healthy person with savings
Someone expecting surgery soon with no savings
Someone with frequent specialist visits
Someone who cannot afford any surprise bill

questions.correct_answer: A healthy person with savings

misconceptions.C: Would pay a lot before coverage

questions.feedback: Low use plus savings to cover the deductible makes a high-deductible plan reasonable.

questions.intro: Compare plans by total yearly cost: 12 × premium + what you pay for care.
questions.question: Plan A: $100 a month, $3,000 deductible. Plan B: $250 a month, $500 deductible. With no medical bills all year, how much less does Plan A cost?

questions.intro: Compare plans by total yearly cost: premiums + what you pay toward allowed charges.
questions.question: Plan A: $1,200 a year in premiums, $3,000 deductible, then 20% coinsurance. Plan B: $3,000 a year in premiums, $500 deductible, then 10% coinsurance. Ana expects $2,000 of allowed in-network charges for the year, all subject to these rules (below both out-of-pocket maximums). Which costs less in total?

choices.text: Plan B, by $450
Plan A, by $1,800
Plan B, by $1,500
Plan A, by $450

questions.correct_answer: Plan A, by $450

questions.intro: Compare plans by total yearly cost: premiums + what you pay toward allowed charges.
questions.question: Plan A: $1,200 premiums, $3,000 deductible, then 20%. Plan B: $3,000 premiums, $500 deductible, then 10%. Ana expects $10,000 of allowed in-network charges for the year, all subject to these rules and below both out-of-pocket maximums. Which costs less?

choices.text: Plan A, by $1,150
Plan B, by $1,150
Plan A, by $1,800
Plan B, by $2,950

questions.correct_answer: Plan B, by $1,150

questions.intro: You can contribute to a health savings account (HSA) only while covered by an HSA-compatible plan. Traditionally that meant a qualifying high-deductible health plan; starting in 2026, bronze and catastrophic plans also count. Money in an HSA is pre-tax and carries over year to year.
questions.question: In 2026 Ana's health plan has a $500 deductible. It is not an HSA-compatible plan: it is not a qualifying high-deductible plan, a bronze plan, or a catastrophic plan. May she contribute to a health savings account (HSA) for that time?

choices.text: Yes; anyone with any health plan may contribute
Yes, once she turns 65
Yes, if she adds a dental plan
No; her plan is not HSA-compatible

questions.correct_answer: No; her plan is not HSA-compatible

misconceptions.B: Invents an age rule; Medicare enrollment actually ends contributions

questions.feedback: Her plan is none of the HSA-compatible types, so she cannot contribute for that time.

questions.intro: Some states run their own health insurance marketplace, such as Get Covered New Jersey; others use HealthCare.gov. Open enrollment is once a year; life events such as losing coverage open a special enrollment period.
questions.question: Ana's job does not offer health insurance. Which statement about shopping for an individual plan in New Jersey is accurate?

choices.text: New Jersey runs its own state marketplace
Only HealthCare.gov serves New Jersey residents
Individual plans can be bought only through social media ads
She must wait until she turns 65

questions.correct_answer: New Jersey runs its own state marketplace

misconceptions.B: Applies to states without their own marketplace

questions.feedback: New Jersey residents use Get Covered New Jersey, the state marketplace.

questions.intro: An EOB is not a bill; it explains what the plan paid and what you may owe. Pay the provider's actual bill after checking that it matches the EOB.
questions.question: An Explanation of Benefits (EOB) says: billed $400; plan discount $150; plan paid $200; patient responsibility $50. What amount does it show Ana is expected to owe the provider?
questions.feedback: $400 − $150 − $200 = $50; pay when the provider's bill arrives and matches.

questions.question: A generic drug costs $10 and the brand-name version costs $45 a month. How much does choosing generic save in a year?
Ana has a sore throat on a weekend. Which choice is usually cheapest for a non-emergency?

choices.text: The hospital emergency room for every minor illness
An urgent care or telehealth visit
Waiting until it becomes an emergency
Buying antibiotics online without a prescription

questions.correct_answer: An urgent care or telehealth visit
questions.feedback: Use urgent care or telehealth for minor problems; the ER is for emergencies.

questions.intro: Most plans cover listed preventive services in network with no cost sharing.
questions.question: Preventive care such as a yearly checkup is often covered at what cost to the patient in network?

choices.text: The full price, since it is optional
Double the usual copay
The whole deductible

questions.feedback: Many preventive services cost $0 in network.

questions.question: A bill shows a charge for a test Ana never had. What should she do?

choices.text: Pay it so her credit is protected
Ignore it, since errors fix themselves
Ask the provider for an itemized bill
Ask the insurer to pay it again

questions.correct_answer: Ask the provider for an itemized bill
questions.feedback: Request an itemized bill and dispute errors with the provider and insurer.

questions.section_skill: Explain auto coverages and calculate what liability limits pay
questions.intro: Liability coverage pays for injuries and damage you cause to others. Limits like 25/50/25 mean $25,000 per injured person, $50,000 for all injuries in one crash, and $25,000 for property damage. The driver can owe anything above the limits.
questions.question: A policy has liability limits of 25/50/25 (thousands). Luis causes a crash that injures one person with $40,000 of medical bills. How much might Luis owe himself?

misconceptions.B: Subtracts the bill from the $50,000 per-accident limit

questions.feedback: The policy pays $25,000 per person; $40,000 − $25,000 = $15,000.

questions.section_skill: Explain auto coverages and calculate what liability limits pay
questions.intro: Collision pays for damage to your car from a crash, minus the deductible. Comprehensive covers non-crash damage (theft, fire, storms, hitting a deer).
questions.question: Which coverage pays to fix Luis's own car after he hits a pole?

choices.text: Collision
Liability, which pays for damage to others
Comprehensive, which covers theft, fire, and hail
Uninsured motorist, for crashes with uninsured drivers

questions.correct_answer: Collision
questions.feedback: Collision covers your car in a crash you cause.

questions.section_skill: Explain auto coverages and calculate what liability limits pay
questions.intro: Comprehensive coverage pays for damage to your car that is not from a crash: theft, fire, falling objects, storms, and hitting an animal.
questions.question: A tree branch falls on Luis's parked car in a storm. Which coverage applies?

choices.text: Collision, because the car was hit by something
Liability, because someone owns the tree
Personal injury protection
Comprehensive

questions.correct_answer: Comprehensive
questions.feedback: Storm damage falls under comprehensive.

questions.section_skill: Explain auto coverages and calculate what liability limits pay
questions.intro: Auto coverages: liability pays for harm you cause to others; collision repairs your car after a crash; personal injury protection (PIP), required in no-fault states such as New Jersey, pays your own medical costs no matter who caused the crash.
questions.question: New Jersey is a "no-fault" state. Which coverage pays the medical bills of Luis and his passengers after a crash, regardless of fault?

choices.text: Collision, which pays to fix his own car
Personal injury protection (PIP)
Liability, which pays for harm he causes to others
Gap coverage, which pays a loan balance

questions.correct_answer: Personal injury protection (PIP)
questions.feedback: PIP pays medical bills for you and your passengers in no-fault states.

questions.section_skill: Explain auto coverages and calculate what liability limits pay
questions.intro: Premiums depend on age, driving record, the car, where you live, coverage chosen, and discounts (good student, safe driver courses, bundling).
questions.question: Which choice usually lowers a teen driver's premium?

choices.text: Good grades and a clean driving record
Driving a powerful sports car
Letting the policy lapse for a few months
Getting a speeding ticket early

questions.correct_answer: Good grades and a clean driving record
questions.feedback: Good-student and safe-driver discounts lower premiums.

questions.section_skill: Who and what each coverage protects
questions.question: Liability coverage pays for…

choices.text: Repairs to your own car only
Your own phone if stolen from the car
Harm you cause to others
Routine oil changes

questions.correct_answer: Harm you cause to others
questions.feedback: Liability covers injuries and damage you cause to others.

questions.section_skill: Who and what each coverage protects
questions.question: In 25/50/25, what does the last 25 mean?

choices.text: $25 deductible for any claim
25 days to report a claim
$25,000 per injured person
$25,000 for property damage

questions.correct_answer: $25,000 for property damage
questions.feedback: The third number is the property damage limit, in thousands.

questions.section_skill: Who and what each coverage protects
questions.question: Luis's collision deductible is $1,000. Repairs cost $3,800. What does insurance pay?

questions.section_skill: Who and what each coverage protects
questions.question: Why is driving without required insurance a serious problem?

choices.text: It is allowed if you drive carefully
It is illegal and leaves you personally liable
It matters only if you cause a crash
Other drivers must pay for the crashes you cause

questions.correct_answer: It is illegal and leaves you personally liable
questions.feedback: Required coverage protects others; driving uninsured brings penalties and personal liability.

questions.section_skill: Who and what each coverage protects
questions.question: An uninsured driver hits Luis. Which coverage helps him?

choices.text: His liability coverage, which pays others
Comprehensive, for theft and storms
Collision, which waives the deductible
Uninsured motorist coverage

questions.correct_answer: Uninsured motorist coverage
questions.feedback: Uninsured motorist coverage protects you when the at-fault driver has no insurance.

questions.intro: Collision pays up to the car's actual cash value minus the deductible. On an older car, it can cost close to what it could ever pay.
questions.question: Luis's car is worth $2,000. Collision coverage costs $600 a year with a $500 deductible. What is the most collision would pay in a total loss?

questions.intro: A higher deductible lowers the premium. Break-even years = extra deductible ÷ yearly savings.

questions.section_skill: Use probability and expected value to evaluate premiums, deductibles, and extended warranties

No; it costs $500 more every year
Yes; it saves about $100 a year
Yes; it saves $650 every year

questions.intro: Across many independent policies, actual losses tend to come close to the expected total (the law of large numbers). A disaster that hits many insured homes at once, such as a hurricane, breaks this pattern.

Accidents raise everyone's premiums equally

questions.intro: When many independent risks are pooled, the total loss is easier to predict. Losses that strike many policyholders at once, such as a regional catastrophe, remain a risk, which is why insurers also buy reinsurance and limit how much they insure in one area.

Apply under a friend's name

questions.unit_title: Consumer Protection, Fraud, and Digital Security
questions.section_skill: Identify common scams and their warning signs, and respond safely
questions.intro: Scam warning signs: a caller pretends to be from a trusted group, there is a problem or a prize, pressure to act now, and a demand to pay in a specific way (gift cards, wire transfer, cryptocurrency, or payment app). Government agencies do not demand gift cards.
questions.question: A caller says he is from the "Social Security office," your number is suspended, and you must pay today with gift cards. Which warning sign appears?

choices.text: The caller uses a polite tone of voice
Demanding payment by gift card
The call comes during business hours
The caller knows that you have a phone

questions.correct_answer: Demanding payment by gift card

misconceptions.A: Politeness is not a warning sign

questions.feedback: Real agencies never ask for payment by gift card.

questions.unit_title: Consumer Protection, Fraud, and Digital Security
questions.section_skill: Identify common scams and their warning signs, and respond safely
questions.intro: In a fake check scam, the scammer overpays with a fake check and asks for the difference back. Banks make deposits available quickly, but the check can bounce days later and the depositor must repay the bank.
questions.question: Rosa sells a bike online for $300. The buyer mails a check for $1,500 and asks her to send back $1,200. Rosa deposits the check, ships the bike, and sends $1,200 by payment app. A week later the check bounces, and the bank takes back the $1,500; the other $300 of it is still in her account at that time. Not counting any bank fees, what has Rosa lost?

choices.text: Nothing, since the bank cleared the check
Only the $300 bike price
$1,200 plus the bike
$1,500 but she keeps the bike

questions.correct_answer: $1,200 plus the bike

misconceptions.A: "Available" does not mean the check is good

questions.feedback: The bank reverses the $1,500: $300 comes from what is left of the deposit, and the $1,200 she sent is gone, along with the bike she shipped.

questions.unit_title: Consumer Protection, Fraud, and Digital Security

questions.question: A job posting pays $40 an hour to "reship packages" after you pay $99 for a starter kit. What is the best response?

choices.text: Pay the fee because good jobs require investment
Give your bank login so they can send pay
Reship the packages to earn trust first
Avoid it; it shows scam signs

questions.correct_answer: Avoid it; it shows scam signs

misconceptions.A: Real employers do not charge to hire

questions.feedback: Paying to get a job and reshipping packages are classic scam signs.

questions.unit_title: Consumer Protection, Fraud, and Digital Security

Share her passwords so they can test them

questions.correct_answer: Close the page and not call

questions.intro: Federal rules (Regulation E) limit debit card losses: $50 if you report within 2 business days of learning of the loss; up to $500 if later; and possibly unlimited if not reported within 60 days after the statement. Many banks offer more protection.

choices.text: $0 in every case

misconceptions.C: Uses the limit for later reporting

questions.intro: Federal rules (Regulation E) limit debit card losses, counted from when you learn of the loss: up to $50 if you report within 2 business days, and up to $500 if you report later. If you do not report unauthorized transfers within 60 days after the statement showing them, you can be liable for later transfers the bank could have stopped.

misconceptions.A: Applies the limit for reporting within 2 business days

questions.feedback: Reporting more than 2 business days after learning of the theft raises the limit to $500.

questions.intro: The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act bars collectors from harassment, threats, and calls before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m. It also gives you the right to dispute a debt and get validation.

Unpaid debts send people to jail

questions.intro: The FTC Cooling-Off Rule lets buyers cancel many sales made at their home for $25 or more, or at temporary locations such as hotel rooms or fairgrounds for $130 or more, within three business days. Saturday counts as a business day; Sundays and federal holidays do not. Some sales, such as real estate, insurance, and emergency repairs, are excluded.
questions.question: A salesperson sells Rosa a $400 vacuum at her home. Under the FTC Cooling-Off Rule, how long does she have to cancel?

choices.text: 30 calendar days
One day
Three business days
No time; home sales are final

questions.correct_answer: Three business days
questions.feedback: A $400 sale at her home is covered: three business days to cancel.

questions.intro: The Fair Credit Billing Act lets you dispute billing errors, including goods not delivered. The issuer must receive your written notice at the address it lists for billing inquiries within 60 days after it sent the statement with the error.

questions.set_title: Consumer rights and where to get help
questions.unit_title: Consumer Protection, Fraud, and Digital Security
questions.intro: A debt collector must give you validation information about the debt. If you dispute in writing within the 30-day validation period after receiving it, the collector must pause collection until it verifies the debt. You can still dispute later, but this pause right applies only within that window.
questions.question: Rosa receives a collector's validation notice about a debt. Within how many days after receiving it can she dispute the debt in writing and make the collector verify it before continuing?
questions.feedback: Dispute in writing within about 30 days after receiving the validation information.

questions.intro: Real pay change ≈ raise − inflation. If prices rise faster than pay, the same paycheck buys less.

It rises by about 2%

It is shrinking

questions.unit_title: Inflation, Interest Rates, and the Economy

questions.intro: The Federal Reserve sets a target for the federal funds rate, which banks charge each other overnight. Changes ripple to credit card, auto, and mortgage rates and to savings yields. Raising rates tends to slow borrowing and cool inflation.

They tend to fall

To print more money

To lower taxes

questions.intro: Taxes pay for many public services. In economics, a "public good" is nonrival (one person's use does not reduce another's) and nonexcludable (hard to keep people from using it). National defense is a classic example. Roads are tax-funded public services, but they can get crowded or charge tolls, so they are not always pure public goods.

questions.section_skill: Identify the key terms of a contract and the questions to ask before signing
questions.intro: A contract is a legally binding agreement. Key parts: the parties, what each promises, the price and fees, the length (term), how it renews, how to cancel, and how disputes are handled. Read every page before signing and keep a copy.

The list of classes offered this month
